fullText:
WASHINGTON, Oct 7 (Reuters) - Democratic Party officials sued US President Donald Trump on Wednesday, seeking a court order blocking his administration from ‌using taxpayer money to pay for election-related TV ads.

The lawsuit, filed by ‌the Democratic National Committee in federal court in Washington, accused Trump of a "blatant violation of the statutory ​ban on the use of appropriations for 'publicity or propaganda purposes.'"

Taxpayer-funded television ads glorifying Trump began airing in late September, sparking a bipartisan backlash.

In a post on his Truth Social site on Monday, Trump said he considered the ads to be "a positive promotion for ‌our Great U.S.A." but that ⁠they would no longer be funded by taxpayers. The White House said this week his MAGA PAC would fund the ads.

The ⁠DNC, the main governing organization of the Democratic Party, said in its lawsuit that the ads continued to air after Trump's comments.

"With less than 30 days remaining before the midterm ​election ​and millions of public dollars apportioned to pay ​for propaganda ads still unspent, ‌the DNC has no choice but to take action in defense of free and fair elections," the lawsuit stated.

The ads ran during football games as recently as Sunday and during other programming. The New York Times reported that Trump personally directed the White House budget director to use taxpayer money for the TV spots, citing sources.

One ‌ad features Trump declaring that "America will never be ​a communist country" while a chorus repeats the ​words "love me." Another combines images of ​Mount Rushmore with footage of Trump praising a "golden age of ‌America."

Another new ad recently has featured ousted ​Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro. ​A source briefed on the matter told Reuters the government-funded ads will end this week.

The White House said Trump's political action committee will not reimburse ​taxpayers for the ads ‌that have run to date.

The ads end with a disclaimer saying they ​were paid for by the US government.

fullText:
The contract for a new plant in Baltimore is the latest linked to the brothers.

President Donald Trump announced a $6.6 billion investment with AI defense company Anduril Industries on Tuesday -- the most recent government funding agreement into a company with investment ties to the president's sons.

The Trump administration announced the Navy will support $2.9 billion of the total cost to help create a new facility in Baltimore County, Maryland, that will manufacture critical parts for the Virginia-class nuclear-powered fast-attack submarine.

"In a tremendous victory for our country and for the city of Baltimore, Anduril is investing $3.7 billion in a state-of-the-art shipyard that will be known forever as Arsenal-2," Trump said at an event announcing the investment.

"Right here in Sparrows Point, you'll build the next generation of American submarines, including autonomous subs, torpedo tubes, and critical components for our cutting edge Virginia-class attack submarines," Trump said.

1789 Capital -- a venture capital firm that lists Donald Trump Jr. as one of six partners along with three founders -- claimed a stake in Anduril in June 2025 from a $2.5 billion investment into the company.

Since that investment, Anduril has been awarded 135 other contracts with the U.S. government and to date has received around $1.8 billion from those agreements, according to active defense contracts posted to SAM.gov, the official system for government contracting.

Anduril did not respond for comment on its contracts or investments from 1789 Capital, though the company has been awarded contracts dating back to 2019, according to USASpending.gov

The company is one of the largest manufacturers to receive an investment from Donald Trump Jr. and his brother Eric Trump, but they are not the only one.

An ABC News analysis found defense companies backed by the president's sons, including Anduril, have now raked in more than $6 billion dollars in active or promised government contracts since those investments were made, according to the government's official contract reporting.

This comes as Congressional Oversight Democrats continue to demand the Pentagon's inspector general investigate the approved deals.

"Refusal to investigate these serious allegations will raise significant concerns about whether your office is able to perform its statutory duty as an independent watchdog over DoD," lawmakers Richard Blumenthal, Elizabeth Warren, Robert Garcia and Tammy Duckworth wrote in a letter to Platte B. Moring, III, the Pentagon's inspector general, in May.

A Pentagon official told ABC News, "No company receives preferential treatment. The War Department always looks for solutions to benefit the warfighter, not any pre-selected entity. Outside affiliations, investors, or political connections play absolutely no role in the Department's funding decisions."

A spokesperson for the Trump brothers denied any wrongdoing.

"Don and Eric are experienced business leaders who have built and invested in businesses across a wide range of industries for decades, long before their father first ran for public office. Their investment decisions are based solely on their independent business judgment and personal convictions and they do not seek to influence, direct, or participate in any government decision, procurement, award, regulatory action, or other governmental process. Attempts to portray their ordinary investment activities as improper are a deliberate distortion of the facts," the spokesperson said.

The White House declined to comment.

Shortly after Trump won the presidency, Donald Trump Jr. was named an adviser for Florida-based drone manufacturer Unusual Machines -- a company which had not previously won any government contracts.

In October 2025, Unusual Machines scored a direct U.S. Dept. of Defense agreement for 3,500 orders of National Defense Authorization Act-compliant motors, with a potential order of 20,000 on the way in 2026.

The Trump brothers are also listed as "notable investors" for the U.S. drone company Powerus, the company announced in March 2026.

Despite not having any government contracts previously, Powerus won its first Air Force purchase order just one month later for an undisclosed amount.

In July, Powerus was awarded up to $90 million for aerial-denial unmanned aircraft systems from the U.S. Air Force.

ABC News asked Powerus if it was concerned at all about the involvement of the Trump brothers in the company, given its active contracts.

"Defense procurement is merit-based. You can't sell the government something that won't protect a soldier, and nobody in the procurement chain risks their career routing a contract to a company whose equipment doesn't work," a spokesperson for Powerus said.

"Neither Donald Trump Jr. nor Eric Trump is an advisor to Powerus, and neither is involved in the company's day-to-day business," the spokesperson continued. "Their interest is indirect, held through American Ventures, an investor in the company."

Trump-linked investments extend into the manufacturing industry, with the brothers combining for more than $1 billion across companies in mining, quantum computing and aerospace.

Oversight Democrats in their letter to the DoD criticized Donald Trump Jr.'s portfolio in raw materials, citing an August 2025 investment into Vulcan Elements, a rare-earth mining company that harvests critical materials for defense manufacturing.

That same month, the Office of Strategic Capital loaned Vulcan Elements $620 million to expand its operation.

Vulcan Elements did not respond for comment when asked about these contracts and the investments from 1789 Capital.

The firm also invested $60 million in Texas-based Firehawk Aerospace, according to firm portfolios provided by PitchBook. In the same month, Firehawk won a $4.9 million Air Force contract to "Advance Hybrid Rocket Engine Development," according to a company press release.

Firehawk would later secure tens of millions more -- $3.2 million in May 2026, an undisclosed "multimillion-dollar" contract with the Air Force Research Laboratory in July and $24 million in Dept. of Defense munitions contracts in August, according to company press releases and active contracts.

Firehawk Aerospace has been awarded government contracts across both the Biden and Trump administrations since the company's founding in 2019.

In a statement to ABC News, Firehawk said its award is "solely the product of engineering expertise and capacity."

"We value the many investors who back that mission and share our conviction that the Nation's arsenal must be built to last. Our focus is the duty in front of us, making the arsenal of the U.S. and our allies stronger," a Firehawk spokesperson said.

ABC News also found 1789 Capital raised $1 billion in revenue generation for California-based PsiQuantum in September of last year, with the company's pre-existing contract with DoD expanding by more than $157 million since then, according to SAM.gov.

PsiQuantum also signed a $100 million letter of intent with the Department of Commerce and another $125 million with the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency in May and July of 2026.

PsiQuantum did not respond when asked for comment on these investments.

Trump-linked investments were found in the automation sector.

Eric Trump said he was named chief strategy adviser for Foundation Future Industries, a humanoid robot startup with the stated aim to develop autonomous soldiers and workers.

Eric Trump touted a $24 million contract in April -- the company's first -- according to Eric Trump and CEO Sankaet Pathal's statements on Fox News. Pathal did not respond for comment on this contract or on Trump's involvement with the company's operations.

ABC News found a $391 million 1789 Capital investment into Hadrian -- a highly automated, AI-driven manufacturing company -- in the early days of 2026.

The company won its first public contracts a few months later in March -- a $39.2 million agreement with the Army for machinery and manufacturing and a $900 million deal with the Navy to create highly automated submarine factories.

Hadrian did not respond for comment when asked about these contracts.

Congressional Democrats continue to sound the alarm over these investments, referring ABC News to their May demand to the Department of Defense to launch an investigation into the president's family.

"We hope that your office will take seriously these latest concerns about corruption in the DoD award process and fulfill your statutory responsibility by initiating a review," the lawmakers wrote in their letter.

title: GOP Senate candidate Mike Rogers breaks with Trump and calls to end Canada tariffs
description:
WASHINGTON — Republican U.S. Senate candidate Mike Rogers appears to be breaking with President Donald Trump on another key issue less than a month before Election Day.
"Drinking a Labatt and watching the Red Wings, man, it just doesn't get any more Michigan than that," Rogers said in a new ad released Oct. 7.
fullText:
WASHINGTON — Republican U.S. Senate candidate Mike Rogers appears to be breaking with President Donald Trump on another key issue less than a month before Election Day.

"Drinking a Labatt and watching the Red Wings, man, it just doesn't get any more Michigan than that," Rogers said in a new ad released Oct. 7. "Here in Michigan, we know that Canada is not our enemy. We need to end this tariff war now."

The statement marks the second time in recent weeks that Rogers spoke out — without criticizing Trump by name — against one of the president's unpopular initiatives. This time, Rogers is calling for an end to Trump's widespread trade war against Canada, America's second-biggest trading partner, while drinking a Canadian beer that's banned from import under the president's latest trade restrictions.

The Republican Senate nominee also split with Trump on the Iran war in late September, saying it "needs to end and end quickly."

Rogers' public shift on tariffs comes amid mounting opposition in Michigan to Trump's tariffs and GOP concerns that voters will reject their candidates up and down the ballot for failing to address cost-of-living concerns. Election Day is Nov. 3, though more than 200,000 Michiganians have already cast absentee ballots.

Trump in recent weeks has derisively called Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney "governor," labeled Canadian officials "nasty" and has complained that Canada is "one of the worst countries in the world to deal with," among other insults.

"They want to have a deal with us. They call us all the time. The problem is that they've treated the United States very unfairly," the Republican president told reporters in late September.

Republican Senate hopeful Rogers debuted the ad the day before he is set to face off in his first debate against Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed in Grand Rapids. The 30-second spot features Rogers wearing a flannel shirt and sitting at a bar stool at Bigg's Bar & Grill on Gratiot Avenue in Chesterfield Township.

More: Most Michigan voters oppose Trump tariffs on Canada, poll shows

A year ago, Rogers accused Democrats of "fear mongering" over Trump's tariffs, and said the president's tariff policy had "put the American people back in the driver's seat."

"President Trump is right to put America First, and tariffs are necessary when countries cheat American workers. But trade isn't one-size-fits-all," Rogers posted on social media on Aug. 29.

In an interview last month, Rogers again defended some of Trump's global tariffs and argued they had helped bring some manufacturing back to the U.S., pointing to General Motors Co.'s decision to move production of the Chevy Silverado pickup truck from Mexico to its Orion Township assembly plant.

Rogers did acknowledge that the tariffs against Canada are going to pinch Michigan consumers and said his team had conversations with the Trump administration about them.

"This is why you want to send somebody back (to Washington) who can have a conversation about what's working for Michigan and what might not work for Michigan, if you send somebody back that all they want to do is get on TikTok and talk about President Trump, we're not going to fix up one single problem," Rogers told The Detroit News.

"But if you send a guy like me back, we're going to have this conversation."

Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed, by contrast, has frequently bashed Trump and Rogers over the ongoing trade war with Michigan's international neighbor, calling the Canadian tariffs "chaotic" and costly.

El-Sayed on Wednesday accused Rogers of flip-flopping again.

"Must have had one too many of those LaBatts, Mike. You cheerled this tariff war from the beginning and you're flip-flopping now because your poll numbers are in free fall," El-Sayed posted on X.com in response to Rogers' ad.

"Donald is the reason we're in a trade war. And he's the reason you're running. Not a serious person."

El-Sayed at an August campaign event said that Canadians "are the only people I know who will preemptively apologize for something they never did ... You gotta be an a------ to pick a trade war with Canada. I'm so sorry, like, they're like the nicest people on Earth."

A Detroit News/WDIV-TV (Channel 4) poll conducted just before Labor Day found that less than one-third (29%) of 600 likely general election voters in Michigan approve of Trump's decision to impose 50% tariffs on $20 billion worth of Canadian goods, including cement, wine, dairy and hockey sticks.

Nearly two-thirds (64%) said they disapprove, according to the survey conducted by the Lansing-based Glengariff Group polling firm Aug. 31 to Sept. 3. The poll has a margin of error of plus or minus four percentage points.

The overwhelming majority of Democratic (93%) and independent (73%) poll participants opposed the tariffs, while most Republicans support them — though there is division within the GOP. About 1 in 4 (24%) of base GOP voters disapprove.

"There is just wholesale opposition to these tariffs," pollster Richard Czuba said of the poll results. "And what really stands out to me is Michiganders understand the financial impact of these tariffs on them."

About 62% of respondents said Trump's tariffs on Canada are bad for Michigan's economy, with 17% saying the tariffs are good. That split is especially pronounced among independent voters, who tend to play a major role in who wins and loses in Michigan elections and 70% of whom said the Canadian tariffs are bad for the state's economy.

Nearly 72% of the likely Michigan voters said the Canadian tariffs would cause an increase in what they pay for goods, according to the poll results.

Some elected Republicans in Michigan have expressed a desire for the Trump administration and Canadian officials to resolve the trade conflict, but they have stopped short of criticizing the president directly.

Republican U.S. Rep. John James, who is running for governor, in an Oct. 6 debate said he's called the Trump administration, specifically talking with the trade ambassador "and saying that we must get back to the table, stop acting like children, and negotiate a reciprocal, fair, and mutually beneficial arrangement to make sure that we can bring our jobs back and protect our industry."

U.S. House hopeful Michael Bouchard of Rochester Hills, a Republican running for James' vacant 10th District seat, said he'd like to see Trump's tariffs on Canadian imports end.

"I don't think our trade conflict with Canada is where we should be focusing a lot of our effort," Bouchard said Oct. 7 in an interview on The Detroit News' Political Insider podcast. "Everybody in Michigan knows Canadians. They're friends with Canada. It's 30 minutes from here to Canada."

Bouchard distinguished his remarks on Canadian tariffs from his support for Trump's global tariffs against China and other countries that are needed to "make sure that Americans are put in a position to succeed.

"But this tariffs on Canada stuff, I've been pretty blunt about that from the beginning," Bouchard said.

GOP U.S. Rep. Tom Barrett of Charlotte, who is locked in a tough reelection fight in his mid-Michigan district, told CNN on Sept. 9 that he's advocating for "cooler heads to prevail" in what he called a "tit for tat" back-and-forth between the U.S. and Canada.

"I want to see us get to a point where we can have mutually beneficial trade arrangements with Canada," Barrett said.

"I'm still hopeful that we'll get there, but that has been my advocacy ― both publicly and behind the scenes ― so that we can move in that direction. And I think it's going to take movement by both sides, the United States and Canada, to get to a mutual arrangement."

The former state lawmaker suggested on CNN that tariffs should be narrowly tailored to balance "anomalies" within U.S. trade arrangements. Barrett pointed to Canada's long-standing tariffs on U.S. dairy products, a policy designed to protect its country's milk, cheese and butter producers from competition.

Barrett said dairy farmers in his district are struggling to make market margins "in no small part because Canada has really manipulated their market there."

U.S. Rep. John Moolenaar, a Caledonia Republican, said last month that he is hoping for an end to the ongoing U.S.-Canada trade dispute, calling some of the negotiations so far counterproductive.

"Unfortunately, what normally is a civil private negotiation working towards agreements has spilled into some name-calling and some things that haven't been as productive as I'd like," Moolenaar said during a telephone town hall on Sept. 1.

"Quite frankly, we've got some work ahead of us," Moolenaar added. "Canada is an important trading partner, and my goal is to see this resolved in a constructive way."

title: Ex-Spurs player Vega set to run for Fifa president
description: Former Tottenham defender Ramon Vega says he intends to run in next year's Fifa presidential election - becoming the first person to confirm they want to challenge Gianni Infantino.
fullText:
Former Tottenham Hotspur defender Ramon Vega says he intends to stand as a candidate in next year's Fifa presidential election.

The 55-year-old is the first person to confirm they want to challenge Gianni Infantino, who has defied calls to step down in the wake of his failed plan to sell off stakes in the World Cup to private investors, which has sparked a major backlash across football.

A former Switzerland centre-back, Vega also played for Celtic and Watford and has worked in finance since retiring from football in 2004.

"I am standing to reunite the global football family, deliver genuine and lasting reform, modernise Fifa for the 21st Century, restore stability and credibility, and rebuild the trust that our game urgently needs," he said.

Meanwhile, Sheikh Salman bin Ibrahim Al Khalifa - president of the Asian Football Confederation - has written to Infantino, distancing himself from an external review of Fifa's governance system.

In his letter - seen by BBC Sport - Sheikh Salman proposes that Fifa's council sets up a working group to examine potential reforms, "rather than being outsourced to an external party".

Last month, Infantino said he was "fully committed to leading Fifa" despite Uefa, Concacaf and the Asian Football Confederation calling for him to quit.

Vega considered running for Fifa's top job in 2015 following the suspension of former president Sepp Blatter.

Four years later he said he would stand against Infantino, but failed to garner enough support to be included in the ballot, having required the backing of five of Fifa's 211 member federations.

Candidates must also be proposed by a member association and have played an active role in the game for two of the past five years, as well as passing an eligibility check by a review committee.

"I am standing because my life has prepared me to serve the game," Vega said in a statement announcing his candidacy.

"Football does not belong to presidents, confederations or administrators. Football is greater than any position, any individual or any institution.

"It is the people's game and belongs to everyone: the players, coaches, referees, supporters, volunteers, clubs, leagues, associations and communities that give football its life.

"It belongs to every child discovering the game, every professional carrying the hopes of a nation, and the billions of supporters whose passion makes football the world's game.

"Football must always come first. Yet for too long, division has fractured our football family.

"The current leadership has demoralised the game. Weak governance has damaged Fifa's credibility and eroded trust across the global football family. We must stop this conflict from escalating.

"Ego-driven battles within football administration must never be allowed to damage those who matter most: the players, coaches, referees and supporters around the world. They are not responsible for these conflicts. They deserve better."

Vega concluded: "Football is in the emergency room, on life support. We cannot wait any longer. Fifa needs a new direction and fundamental reform.

"We must reunite the football family, restore trust, bring stability and modernise Fifa's governance. This requires decisive change - not cosmetic adjustments."

Infantino should have no place in future of football - Pinto

It comes with Sheikh Salman appearing to soften his stance towards Infantino just two months after the AFC president signed a joint letter with the heads of Uefa and Concacaf accusing the Fifa president of breaking trust "through deception" over his Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) plan.

At the time, the three confederations said any review of Fifa's governance must be "conducted by a fully independent third party".

Now, however, Salman says he believes the process should be "driven by the football institutions themselves, rather than being outsourced to an external party".

He added: "I believe there is value in taking this opportunity to consider constructively whether Fifa's existing governance arrangements can be strengthened.

"The issue is not necessarily whether this requires a wholesale redesign of Fifa's governance system."

Fifa's council meets in Zurich next week for the first time since the FFE plan emerged in July.

title: Sen. Tillis calls deciding vote for Hegseth the 'biggest regret' of his career
description:
— Republican Sen. Thom Tillis says in a new book that his deciding vote to confirm Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth in January 2025 is the “biggest regret of my career” and that he also “should’ve stopped” Robert F. Kennedy Jr. from becoming Health and Human Services secretary in the early days of President Donald Trump’s second term. 
In “How to Lose Friends and Antagonize Presidents,” to be published Tuesday, the North Carolina senator defends his decision at the time to not be “the lone voice in the wilderness” preventing Trump’s nominees from confirmation.
fullText:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Republican Sen. Thom Tillis says in a new book that his deciding vote to confirm Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth in January 2025 is the "biggest regret of my career" and that he also "should've stopped" Robert F. Kennedy Jr. from becoming Health and Human Services secretary in the early days of President Donald Trump's second term.

In "How to Lose Friends and Antagonize Presidents," to be published Tuesday, the North Carolina senator defends his decision at the time to not be "the lone voice in the wilderness" preventing Trump's nominees from confirmation. But Tillis makes clear he was always skeptical of allegations about Hegseth's turbulent management style, treatment of women and excessive drinking. Hegseth denied all the allegations.

"I know for a fact that there are others like me," Tillis writes, "Republicans who agreed to go along with the early demands of the Trump team no matter how ridiculous they were, believing that failing to do so would mean the end of their political career, and who now see that things have gone way too far."

He writes that he can count at least 30 of his GOP colleagues who have "expressed reservations (to put it mildly) about many of the president's actions in private. Then, when the reporters showed up with their cameras and microphones, they'd have nothing but nice things to say."

Tillis, who announced last year that he would not run for reelection in a "breaking point" with the president on his sweeping tax and spending cuts package, is publishing the book in his final months in office. He joins a long list of Republicans who have ratcheted up their public denunciations of Trump once they had less to lose politically.

Still, Tillis mostly deflects full blame from Trump, saying, "my beef is not with him, but the idiots he's got working for him." He calls the president "an amazing political talent."

At the same time, he warns of a slippery slope toward authoritarianism and urges his colleagues to "wake up" and push back on Trump more often, for their own political good. Executive overreach, he says, doesn't work and sooner or later, "comes back to bite the majority party in the ass."

Tillis also predicts a "bloodbath" for Republicans in November's midterm elections.

"All along, we've had multiple chances to get off the path and avoid the giant bronze monster chasing us down," he writes.

The book is filled with cuss words and condemnations. He criticizes Trump's tariffs, the aggressive immigration raids that Tillis says were an effort to "intentionally sow disorder" and the Iran war, which he initially supported. He said the war can only end with a coalition of willing nations and if Trump gets "Pete Hegseth the hell out of the way."

Tillis pushed Hegseth's confirmation vote late into the evening on Jan. 24, 2025, as he weighed his decision, talking to the White House, people who had worked with Hegseth and Hegseth himself. In the end, he said he couldn't corroborate the worst allegations and would support Hegseth's confirmation. His vote brought the total to 50-50, and Vice President JD Vance broke the tie.

On his vote for Kennedy, Tillis writes that "I guess it's easy to say now, but I'm the one who has to live with that vote and all the havoc Kennedy's tenure has caused the country as a result."

On both votes, he says he didn't want to be the deciding factor.

"I had no intention of letting my colleagues outsource their courage to me while they pretended to go along with the questionable nomination President Trump had put forward," he writes.

If you oppose Trump on everything, "you lose all influence," Tillis says. "If you oppose him and lose, you are in even worse shape."

He strongly criticizes several of Trump's other initial picks for the Cabinet in the book, including former Director of National Intelligence Tulsi Gabbard, former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick.

Tillis's surprise announcement in June 2025 that he wouldn't be running for reelection came as he escalated criticism against Trump and his " Big Beautiful Bill " of tax and spending cuts. Trump attacked Tillis on social media after the senator said he couldn't support the bill's cuts to Medicaid. Tillis says he thought to himself, "I'm done."

"Everyone reaches a breaking point," he writes.

He texted the president asking him to look for his replacement in the Senate, to which Trump replied "I am! DJT."

In May 2026, Trump again attacked Tillis, calling him a "QUITTER!" on social media, among other insults.

Tillis ends the book with a profanity-laced text he sent to the president in response.

"I care if you fail and right now we are failing," Tillis wrote to Trump.

title: 4 ways the midterm elections could turn out, with a month to go
description:
Democrats are heading into the last month of the midterm elections campaign with ambitions going deeper and deeper into red territory, while Republicans are grim about their hopes of holding on to either chamber of Congress.
Historically, the opposition party almost always makes gains in the midterms, and President Donald Trump is less popular than ever. His support has weakened especially with independents in high-quality polls and among swing demographics that propelled his 2024 majority.
Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post. 
Republicans have also tended to underperform when Trump isn’t on the ballot because more consistent voters have shifted toward the Democrats.
fullText:
Democrats are heading into the last month of the midterm elections campaign with ambitions going deeper and deeper into red territory, while Republicans are grim about their hopes of holding on to either chamber of Congress.

Historically, the opposition party almost always makes gains in the midterms, and President Donald Trump is less popular than ever. His support has weakened especially with independents in high-quality polls and among swing demographics that propelled his 2024 majority.

Republicans have also tended to underperform when Trump isn't on the ballot because more consistent voters have shifted toward the Democrats. More Democrats voted in this year's primaries - a sign that they are also more likely to turn out now, with early and mail voting already underway in 43 states leading up to Election Day on Nov. 3.

The Democrats' lead in national and battleground polls has expanded since Labor Day. There are reasons to suspect polls could be overestimating Democrats' strength, though surveys did not systematically favor Democrats in the last two midterms.

Republicans' main advantage is money. GOP campaigns and allies are outspending Democrats in almost all the most contested races, thanks in large part to more than $180 million that has been pumped in from Trump's war chest since Labor Day.

The outcome will define the remainder of Trump's presidency - the fate of his legislative ambitions and the pressure of oversight investigations. It will also immediately set the stage for the 2028 presidential primaries, with both parties' hopefuls reading the results for clues to the electorate's mood.

Here are four possible ways the midterms could broadly shake out.

In the House, Republicans hold the slimmest of majorities, with 218 seats (and one independent who caucuses with them) to the Democrats' 214. The GOP is on defense in 16 seats rated toss-ups by the Cook Political Report, compared with six for Democrats. On Sept. 25, Cook shifted 15 races toward the Democrats and projected them to take over the House.

Anticipating a favorable environment, Democrats went into the cycle planning to expand the House battlefield by recruiting competitive candidates to run in typically safe GOP districts held by incumbents unaccustomed to tough races or dragged down in scandals. On Friday, they continued widening their targets, adding eight districts that voted for Trump by double digits in 2024. They added six more races on Monday, including seats in Arkansas and Tennessee and a Nevada district that backed Trump by 14 points. The latest additions bring their total targets to 46.

If Democrats win the popular vote by 10 points this year - their current average lead in polls - they would pick up a projected 33 seats, according to Mindset, a Washington advisory firm. That would place this year's gains between the Democratic pickups in 2006 (31 seats) and 2018 (40 seats).

"Democrats are on offense; Republicans are running scared - even in deep-red territory," said Rep. Suzan DelBene (Washington), chair of the House Democrats' campaign arm. "Voters are fed up with Republicans' broken promises and ready for change in Congress."

In the Senate, Republicans hold a 53-47 majority and were favored to keep control earlier this year.

Now, most polls put Democrats ahead in the most contested races: Alaska, Iowa, Maine, Michigan, New Hampshire, Ohio and Texas. They're more strongly favored to win North Carolina, where former governor Roy Cooper (D) leads former Republican National Committee chairman Michael Whatley, and Georgia, where Rep. Mike Collins (R) hasn't come close to catching Sen. Jon Ossoff (D). On Friday, the main Republican Senate super PAC canceled its remaining spending in North Carolina.

Beyond the battlegrounds, Republicans have shown concern about incumbents in Kansas, which hasn't elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1932, and Nebraska, which Trump won by 20 points in 2024. Sen. Roger Marshall (R-Kansas), an obstetrician, is under fire for his history of suing patients to collect unpaid bills, leading to some arrests. He faces megachurch pastor Adam Hamilton (D). Nebraska independent Dan Osborn has been slamming Sen. Pete Ricketts (R) for pardoning a man convicted of sexual assault when he was governor.

In the most extreme scenario, some political professionals imagine the wave wiping out Sen. Darline Graham (R-South Carolina) or Sen. Ashley Moody (R-Florida).

The Senate does not as consistently turn against the president - Republicans added two seats in the upper chamber in 2018. This year's map has more GOP-held seats in contention, but taking the majority would require the Democrats to hold Georgia and Michigan, pick up North Carolina and Maine, plus win two out of 12 seats in states that Trump won by at least 13 points.

In the House, Democrats need a net gain of only three seats. But across decades, partisan gerrymandering has steadily shrunk the battlefield, so even an electoral swing of similar magnitude to past cycles might not flip as many seats.

This cycle, Republicans tilted the field further in their direction by redrawing congressional maps ahead of the customary once-a-decade redistricting. Republicans hoped to move 16 districts to the right with new maps in Texas (five districts), Florida (four), Ohio (two), Alabama, Louisiana, Missouri, North Carolina and Tennessee (one each). Democrats responded with five districts in California, and courts overturned the Missouri map and added a Democratic-leaning seat in Utah, cutting the Republicans' theoretical edge to nine.

But many of those redrawn seats are shaping up to be less solid than Republicans had hoped. Democrats are still contesting four redrawn seats in Texas and another four in Florida. They hope to keep one or two affected districts in Ohio (held by Reps. Marcy Kaptur and Greg Landsman), plus the one in North Carolina (Rep. Don Davis).

"People want to make predictions, but there's a lot of toss-up races that are not decided yet," Republican pollster John McLaughlin said. "The sides are forming where the Democratic/anti-Republican vote is coming together and Republicans are losing the ability to recover swing voters. That's concerning."

In the previous midterms of 2022, the roles were reversed: Republicans were confident the unpopular sitting president would sweep their candidates into power despite their flaws, and were dismayed when that wave failed to materialize. Now, they are hoping for a similar dynamic, only the other way around.

If Republicans pull an upset, they'll be able to thank the Senate map that puts them mostly on their home turf and gerrymandering for padding their cushion in the House. The polls would have to be significantly off, which could be because Democrats were more eager to answer the phone, Republicans were less likely to participate, or pollsters misjudged who would turn out to vote.

Trump political adviser Chris LaCivita summed up the Republicans' path to victory as: "money, message, motivation and the president's ability to defy conventional wisdom."

Republicans outspent Democrats in every Senate battleground in September and also led in future reservations though Election Day, according to media tracker AdImpact.

Republicans are also hoping to benefit in races where further-left Democrats won their primaries. Those Democrats include Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan and House candidates William Lawrence in Michigan and Randy Villegas in California.

The GOP's midterms convention and Trump's stump speeches have sought to portray the Democrats as extreme and tie the entire party to self-described socialists who won in some areas.

And as much as Democrats want to make the race about Trump (and he does, too), at least some Republicans may be able to outperform his unpopularity. Candidates from Iowa to Florida have started removing references to Trump from their websites and breaking with the president on immigration and the Iran war.

Elections are run at the local level, with no role for the federal government. The Trump administration has made multiple attempts to change voting procedures for the midterms, but those efforts were held up in court or died in Congress.

"It has been a roller coaster," Eric Fey, the Democratic elections director in St. Louis, said at a recent meeting of elections officials.

Each election cycle features emergency litigation over mishaps at voting locations (often resulting in extended hours), recounts in close races and post-election audits. Administrators and law enforcement officials are also on the lookout for cyberattacks or disruptions such as bomb threats. They conduct drills and simulations to anticipate how things could go wrong and practice how to respond.

"The threat landscape, as we view it this year, is cyber, physical, logistical, reputational and somewhat emergent legal," said Michael Moore, the chief information security officer for the Arizona secretary of state's office. "We design exercises to give election officials the most miserable Election Day we can possibly imagine. That way, when they actually have an election day, they're prepared for everything."

This year, election administrators are especially concerned about interference from the federal government. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin has said the administration has no plans to send immigration officers to polls, while FBI Director Kash Patel would not rule out sending his agents to voting sites.

"While I anticipate that we likely will have monitors and there could be incidents at or around voting locations, we're going to make sure that we have boots on the ground to make sure that voters are not disrupted in that process and that they can cast a ballot," said Dean Logan, the registrar-recorder and county clerk for Los Angeles County, the country's largest election jurisdiction.

Monica Gordon, the clerk in Cook County, Illinois (home to Chicago), added: "We're moving forward as usual, but we plan for anything. Our contingencies have contingencies."

Right-wing activists have called for Trump to take more severe steps, such as trying to claim emergency powers over elections. Trump has repeatedly challenged the legitimacy of elections he and his party lost. Congressional Democrats and allied lawyers have also prepared research and drills to be ready for any attempts to use federal power to interfere with the results, as Trump attempted after losing in 2020.

"A lot of people would say that we need to just go rogue and declare this radical emergency," Tina Peters, a former Colorado county clerk who was released on parole in June after serving some of her sentence for tampering with voting equipment, said Wednesday during a meeting of online activists. "There are already orders and laws in place that allow them to do what they need to do."

title: Immigration, AR-15 bans and climate lawsuits land before the Supreme Court
description:

fullText:
The US Supreme Court opens its new term on Monday with the Trump administration's immigration crackdown, gun rights and the fate of climate change lawsuits on the docket.

The session opens one month ahead of a crucial midterm vote that could see President Donald Trump's Republican Party lose its majority in the House of Representatives and possibly even the Senate.

Losing control of Congress would force the president to have to rely even more on the conservative-dominated top court to push through his policies.

Not that it has always been in lockstep with Trump.

Trump suffered stinging defeats this year over his tariffs and bid to restrict birthright citizenship, sparking tirades by the president against the court, particularly the three justices he appointed during his first White House term.

"I gave them the position of a lifetime, and they vote against me often," he told Time magazine in a recent interview.

At the same time, the 6-3 conservative majority has allowed Trump to vastly expand his executive powers and handed him a number of victories on what is known as the emergency docket, where cases are fast-tracked without oral arguments.

At the end of September, for example, in an immigration case in which the three liberal justices dissented, the court allowed the administration to continue for the time being to deport undocumented migrants to countries that are not their own.

The court will hear oral arguments in that case during the fall term and a ruling in the administration's favor could open the floodgates to more so-called "third country" deportations.

More than 25,000 people have been sent to third countries since Trump returned to office after reaching secret agreements with some 35 nations, most of them in Latin America and Africa.

- 'Concerned about the future' -

In another immigration case, the court will weigh a new practice of automatically detaining undocumented migrants -- even those who have lived in the United States for years -- instead of releasing them while their cases are being adjudicated.

"The Trump administration is interpreting that mandatory detention statute in a way that no administration has ever done in the 30 years since that statute was enacted," said Cecillia Wang, the national legal director of the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU). "It's to pressure people to, as the government puts it, self-deport."

The opening case of the term may decide whether climate suits brought by local governments against oil companies for their role in global warming can proceed or whether federal law should prevail.

On the election front, the Supreme Court will take up an Arizona law requiring proof of citizenship when registering to vote.

Trump and fellow Republicans have baselessly claimed for years that many non-citizens vote in US elections but studies have shown the actual number is insignificant.

Gun ownership returns to the court in a case challenging state or local bans on certain semi-automatic weapons such as AR-15s.

The role of religion in public education will be tested when the justices hear a case involving a Catholic preschool in Colorado that denies admission to children of LGBTQ+ parents.

The question in the case is "whether they have a right to receive taxpayer dollars without following the non-discrimination rules that apply to everyone else," said Dan Mack, director of the ACLU's Program on Freedom of Religion and Belief.

On the eve of the new term, Justice Samuel Alito, a staunch conservative, gave a rare public interview in which he told Fox News Sunday he was "concerned about the future of the court."

"There has been a concerted effort to intimidate the court and justices on the court to try to influence us to decide cases," the 76-year-old Alito said.

A recent Gallup survey found that Americans' views of the Supreme Court are at their least positive since the organization began polling on the institution in 1972.

Only 34 percent of US adults approve of the job the court is doing, essentially unchanged from the record-low 33 percent approval tallied in July, Gallup said.

title: Poll shows Latino voters swinging away from Trump and Republicans
description:
NBC News
Latino voters helped propel Donald Trump back to the White House. Now, they are turning on him, according to a new NBC News/Telemundo poll — a shift that gives Democrats a major opportunity to capitalize in a 2026 election that could hinge on states and districts with sizable Latino populations.
Like the broader electorate, Latino voters are racked by major concerns about high prices and Trump’s approach to immigration enforcement. The president’s approval rating sits at 27% among Latino voters. Two-thirds say his administration’s deportation policies have gone too far and three-quarters disapprove of how he has handled the economy and the cost of living.
fullText:
Latino voters helped propel Donald Trump back to the White House. Now, they are turning on him, according to a new NBC News/Telemundo poll — a shift that gives Democrats a major opportunity to capitalize in a 2026 election that could hinge on states and districts with sizable Latino populations.

Like the broader electorate, Latino voters are racked by major concerns about high prices and Trump’s approach to immigration enforcement. The president’s approval rating sits at 27% among Latino voters. Two-thirds say his administration’s deportation policies have gone too far and three-quarters disapprove of how he has handled the economy and the cost of living.

There are clear signs his party is paying the price.

A greater share of Latino voters hold negative views of the Republican Party than at any time since 2016, and Democrats have leads on issues like dealing with the economy, immigration, the cost of living, corruption and healthcare. Two years ago, Latino voters gave Trump a 4-point edge over then-Vice President Kamala Harris on handling the economy. Today, they give Democrats a 21-point advantage on the same question.

Against that backdrop, Democrats have a 24-point lead on whom Latino voters want to see in control of Congress, 59%-35%.

That’s double the lead they had among Latino voters at this point in 2024, though not quite at the heights the party enjoyed at this time in 2018, according to NBC News polling from just before that election.

Nearly a fifth of Latino voters who backed Trump in 2024 say they do not prefer a Republican-controlled Congress, with 14% saying they support Democrats and 8% unsure in their preference.

The shifts come after the Republican Party made Trump’s 2024 gains among Latino voters central to its plans to keep the House majority. In Florida and Texas, the party drew new, heavily Latino districts that looked deep red by the 2024 results — but many are shaping up to be competitive in the midterms as Latino voters’ preferences have changed. Statewide races in Texas, Nevada and more will also be shaped by the evolving Latino vote, though it will not move as one bloc everywhere in the country.

The poll results, collected Sept. 21-28, “indicate a striking reversal of Republican gains with Latino voters and point to trouble ahead for Republican candidates in the midterms,” said Democratic pollster Aileen Cardona-Arroyo of Hart Research Associates, who conducted the poll with Republican pollster Micah Roberts and his firm, Public Opinion Strategies. Latino voters comprised around a tenth of the total vote in recent midterm elections.

Roberts referred to Latino voters as “the swingiest of swing groups,” calling the reversal since 2024 “stunning.”

“What we can really say from this data is that 2024 was the outlier,” he said, adding: “Trump is a central figure. He’s had real consequences on our politics, and without his presence, I think none of these changes would be evident in the data among Latinos.”

But the results among Latino voters are not all good news for Democrats, who have not seen their party’s image improve in two years. And while Democrats have a midterm lead, Republicans are pulling more Latino support than in any NBC News poll before the 2024 election cycle, too, dating back to 2012.

“Despite a more favorable environment for Democrats, any Democratic gains this November will be driven largely more by opposition to Trump and the economic environment than by support for Democrats,” Arroyo-Cardona said.

Latino voters overwhelmingly disapprove of the president’s handling of the cost of living (78%), the economy (74%), foreign policy (68%) and immigration (69%). Trump’s best issue of the five tested is border security — where 39% approve and 58% disapprove of his handling.

His marks on foreign policy, the economy and cost of living are significantly lower than where then-President Joe Biden sat with Latino voters in September 2022, when Democrats had a better-than-expected midterm result despite losing control of the House. Then, 60% disapproved of Biden’s handling of the cost of living and 54% disapproved of his handling of the economy.

Nearly two-thirds (65%) of Latino voters say the president’s policies have hurt economic conditions, compared with 23% who say his policies have helped and 11% who say they haven’t made much of a difference.

Among Latino independents, just 10% believe his policies have helped the economy, while 72% believe his policies have hurt it.

Meanwhile, inflation and the cost of living ranked as the most important issue to 33% of Latino voters. That made it the top issue in the survey — and a majority (52%) ranked it as the most or second-most important issue.

Latino voters who say the cost of living is the most important issue also prefer a Democratic Congress by 22 points. That’s a shift from the 2024 poll, when Republicans had a 4-point edge among these voters.

A sizable majority of Latinos (63%) say their family’s income is falling behind the cost of living, while 25% say it is staying even and 11% say it is going up faster than the cost of living, similar to findings in 2024.

Luisa Santiago, a 59-year-old Florida retiree who participated in the survey, told NBC News in a subsequent interview that she voted for Trump in 2024 after a lifetime of voting for Democrats and convinced many of her friends to do the same. She was frustrated with the Democrats on the economy and on transgender issues.

“It was a big deal when we voted for Republicans, and then we feel like it was a complete mistake,” she said, calling Trump a “disappointment.”

“I’m more embarrassed than my friends because I was the one who convinced them to vote for him,” she added.

Santiago lambasted the president’s deportation policies as “brutal” and “cold,” while also saying the difficult economic climate is weighing heavily on her and her family.

While immigration didn’t rank as highly on the priority list, Latino voters expressed similar frustration with Trump’s hard-edged deportation policies.

Two-thirds say Trump’s immigration enforcement measures have gone too far, 22% say he’s struck the right approach, and 9% say he hasn’t gone far enough.

While 83% support deporting all undocumented immigrants who have committed serious crimes, just 37% support deporting every undocumented immigrant in the U.S.

Roberts, the Republican pollster, pointed to the difference between support for deporting serious criminals and deporting everyone in America illegally as he imagined “what might have been” for Republicans.

“There is support for a certain level of immigration enforcement, but the Latino electorate believes it’s gone way too far,” he added.

In the poll, 31% of Latino voters say they or someone close to them started carrying identification over concerns about ICE enforcement, while 27% say they know someone who has been deported or detained by ICE in the last two years.

Eighteen percent say they or someone close to them has considered leaving the U.S. over the last two years over concerns about ICE enforcement, and 17% say they or someone close to them has considered not voting in person this year because of concerns about ICE.

Maria, a Florida voter in her 20s who responded to the poll, told NBC News in a follow-up interview that Trump has “fallen short” in the two years since she voted for him. She declined to share her last name while discussing politics.

She highlighted frustration on the economy and on deportations, arguing that while Trump promised to deport the worst of the worst, “I’ve had many friends, family members deported.”

“They were supposed to be here. They had paperwork, and it didn’t matter. And now they can never come back. One of my friend’s grandpas didn’t even get deported to his home country. He got deported to Mexico instead of Cuba,” she later added.

The numbers for Trump and Republicans could spell trouble in November in states and districts with sizable Latino populations.

“In a lot of the heavily Hispanic and Latino districts across the country that Trump and Republicans did well, and better than ever in, in 2024, you’re going to see that reversal,” said Roberts, the Republican pollster, noting Trump’s tough numbers on immigration and the cost of living.

“This entire poll is full of very clear directional signals that Latinos have turned from 2024 and are ready to make a different choice with regard to who’s in control of Congress,” Roberts said.

Democrats’ 24-point lead on the generic congressional ballot is twice as large as their margin in the 2024 version of the poll. But it’s not nearly as wide as the 43-point lead the party enjoyed at this point in the 2018 midterms.

Latino voters also now say Democrats would better handle the cost of living and the economy by significant margins, erasing the advantages Trump and Republicans have enjoyed in past elections.

Latino voters favor Democrats to handle other issues, and they break even on which party would better handle border security. More voters also say Democrats are more likely than Republicans to share their values and address the concerns of the Hispanic community.

Amid the economic frustrations, voters are also more motivated to head to the polls in November. A sizable majority (72%) rank themselves a 10 out of 10 in terms of interest in November’s elections, compared with 54% at this time in 2024. Meanwhile, 62% say they are more motivated to vote this year than in midterms past.

And a majority (54%) say their midterm vote is meant to send a signal of opposition to Trump, while 21% say they want to signal their support for Trump and 23% say their vote is not about sending a signal to the president either way.

While the poll results offer plenty of short-term upside for Democrats, they also outline longer-term changes trending against the party.

While Latino voters’ negative views of the GOP have jumped since 2024, views of the Democratic Party have not improved. Now, 62% of Latino voters have negative views of the Republican Party, a 16-point increase from two years ago, while 42% have a negative view of the Democratic Party, a 4-point increase from 2024.

“I’m still wary about the Democratic Party because I don’t really know that much other than what I was fed,” said Maria, the Florida voter in her 20s, before adding that she’s still leaning toward voting for Democrats: “I feel like I have to put my faith in them now to fix things.”

She said she voted for Trump in 2024 in large part because her family instilled a fear of socialism and Democrats in her.

The poll found that socialism remains underwater with Latino voters — 13% feel positively about it and 41% view socialism negatively, with 38 feeling neutral about socialism.

Cardona-Arroyo, the Democratic pollster, noted that the party has work to do after the midterms to develop a broader message.

“What do Democrats do to move beyond this place where they’re running on opposition to the Republican Party, which I think will work in ’26,” Cardona-Arroyo said. “It’s sort of an open question of whether that will work in ’28.”

The NBC News/Telemundo poll surveyed 800 registered Latino voters Sept. 21-28 via a mix of telephone interviews and an online survey sent via text messages. Overall, 20% of the interviews were conducted in Spanish. The poll has a margin of error of plus or minus 3.5 percentage points.

title: Trump predicts a ‘big surprise’ for Republicans as he rallies voters in Ohio

fullText:
VANDALIA, Ohio — President Donald Trump rallied Saturday for Republicans in Ohio’s competitive races for Senate and governor, predicting that the party will defy expectations in a choppy midterm election climate.

“I think we’re going to have a big surprise, because they don’t know what’s happening,” Trump said while speaking onstage inside a high school gymnasium near Dayton.

“Just get out and vote,” Trump added. “If you do that, we’re going to win, and we’re going to win big. And we’re going to shove it up their ass.”

The visit, part of what White House officials have told NBC News will be a push through at least 17 states between now and Nov. 3, was aimed at boosting Sen. Jon Husted and GOP gubernatorial nominee Vivek Ramaswamy.

Trump, who won Ohio three times by comfortable margins, opened his speech with praise for both before moving into broader remarks to promote himself and his administration. He also offered support for local Rep. Mike Turner and for several House candidates in attendance, including Derek Merrin, the Republican running against longtime Democratic Rep. Marcy Kaptur in northwest Ohio.

Husted’s bid to keep the Senate seat — which he was appointed to after JD Vance was elected vice president — has become a subject of concern among Republicans in Ohio and Washington. In August, the National Republican Senatorial Committee warned in a memo that Husted’s past enthusiasm for building data centers was hurting his campaign. Others have expressed worries that Husted, who has long wanted to be governor, has not put his full heart into the race.

The battle is one of the most expensive and competitive Senate races in the country this fall. Along with a handful of other key contests, the clash between Husted and Brown could determine partisan control of the chamber. This week, the Senate Leadership Fund, a super PAC affiliated with Senate Majority Leader John Thune of South Dakota, poured another $14 million into Ohio to prop up Husted, bringing the group’s investment in the state to $93 million.

“Sen. Jon Husted votes to put Ohio first, and he votes all the time,” Trump said before relating conversations he’s had with Thune and others: “They think he’s phenomenal.”

The high school gym where Trump spoke Saturday night was a smaller venue than has been typical for his rallies. The home court of the Butler High School Aviators seats up to 5,000. There were several stretches of empty seats in upper bleachers as Trump took the stage — and many more by the time he finished speaking 93 minutes later.

In Ohio and elsewhere, Republicans are wrestling with how to win at a time when polls show Trump and the war with Iran are highly unpopular and when voters most loyal to Trump might stay home because he’s not on the ballot.

“As a lifelong Republican who’s voted in every election since I was 18 and in every primary election as a Republican, I have real concerns that we’re going to be able to turn out the every-four-year Trump voter,” Nick Owens, a former GOP chair in Ohio’s Brown County and former member of the state Board of Education, told NBC News last month. “I have real concerns that those voters just will not come to the polls.”

Trump acknowledged that dynamic explicitly Saturday and repeated an argument he’s been making on the campaign trail this fall.

“When I run, we win,” Trump said. “But for some reason, when I don’t run, they draw 44% less people. So what I’m going to do is ask you to just pretend that I’m running, because if we do, and if you draw the people, you’re going to win, and we’re going to win big.”

Husted, speaking to reporters before the rally, described Trump as a unique asset in his race.

“Well, he won Ohio by 11 points in the last election, and if we get those same voters to turn out in this election, we’ll win,” Husted said.

Alex Triantafilou, the Ohio GOP chair, told NBC News that the rally was “hugely important” in the effort to motivate those low-propensity, Trump-loyal voters.

“We know in Ohio that if we turn out the same electorate that we turned out in 2024, that we’ll win every race,” Triantafilou said in an interview. “Nobody speaks to that crowd better than President Trump.”

The Saturday rally included a cameo from Jon Gruden, the former NFL coach who years ago was a teammate of Husted’s on the University of Dayton football team.

“Jon Husted is a lot more than my friend,” an animated Gruden told the audience. “He was a great player. … He will never quit on you or anybody.”

Trump marveled about Husted’s football-playing days, of which he said he was unaware until hearing about them from Gruden.

“Nobody told me you were a great athlete,” Trump said, before taking a jab at his Democratic rival: “And Brown was not — he was not an athlete. That guy can’t tie his shoes.”

For its part Saturday, the Brown team sent a mobile billboard linking Husted’s support for the Iran war to higher gas prices through Dayton and on the streets near the rally.

“Jon Husted has turned his back on working families — he’s only looking out for his billionaire buddies and special interests,” Brown said in a statement from his campaign.

Ohio also is home to what polls show is a close race to succeed term-limited Republican Gov. Mike DeWine. Ramaswamy faces Democrat Amy Acton, a physician who served as the state’s health director under DeWine. Ohioans have not elected a Democrat as governor in 20 years, but at a time when high prices are top of mind for voters, there are questions about the billionaire Ramaswamy’s appeal, especially in rural parts of the state.

Ramaswamy, like Husted, addressed the crowd early during the rally, and Trump invited both to return to the stage during his speech. Trump introduced Ramaswamy by noting how he had briefly run against him for the 2024 Republican presidential nomination.

“He was a nasty guy,” Trump said of Ramaswamy. “But you know what? He was smart. He loves the state. He’s actually got a great heart.”

Compared with Husted, Ramaswamy was otherwise less of a focus of Trump’s remarks. Trump, for example, criticized Senate Democrats who this week blocked Husted’s Ratepayer Protection Act, which aims to rein in higher utility costs associated with power-hungry data centers.

Republicans, Trump said, are “taking historic action to ensure that Big Tech data centers benefit local communities.”

Trump then made the argument for data centers, despite the fears it could be a losing issue for Husted.

“We want them,” Trump said. “Look, there’s so much money to be made for Ohio. You can’t just turn them off. They’ll go to China.”

Trump also recited the lyrics to the 1968 Al Wilson song “The Snake” — a recurring, crowd-pleasing bit in his rally speeches — with a new, localized twist. Trump dedicated the song, which he uses as an allegory for trusting communities that welcome immigrants, to nearby Springfield, Ohio.

The city became a flashpoint in the 2024 presidential election after Trump repeated the unsubstantiated and racially charged claim that Haitian immigrants in the city were eating pets.

At another point, the crowd broke into chants of “four more years” for the term-limited president.

“I’d love to do the four-more-year thing,” Trump responded in a teasing tone before suggesting that the press would overplay his remarks.

“We’re driving them totally crazy,” Trump said, referring to the media. “But I love doing it. I love being with you. I really do.”

fullText:
Four weeks to Election Day, a growing number of House Republicans privately fear their chances of holding onto the majority are vanishing and have begun focusing on how to limit the size of a potential Democratic wave.

Inside the House GOP, Republicans have watched with alarm as President Donald Trump’s approval ratings have sunk in their own internal polling — including on traditionally red turf — over the last two weeks, according to more than a dozen people familiar with the discussions.

Now, the House GOP is entering triage mode. Republicans are discussing pulling money from once-competitive races they see as too difficult to win, including Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks in Iowa, Rep. Tom Kean in New Jersey and an open seat in Nebraska, according to three people familiar with the talks.

But the GOP does have a huge cash advantage, and not all Republicans are pessimistic. Speaker Mike Johnson is “absolutely still convinced” that he can hang onto the House and is not taking any seats “off his board,” according to a political aide. Johnson just returned from New Jersey and is planning a rally with Miller-Meeks in Iowa next week, according to his team.

The House GOP’s campaign arm, too, strenuously denies that the majority is lost.

“Thirty days out, House Republicans are on offense, and we’re outspending Democrats in the final stretch in every race,” National Republican Congressional Committee spokesperson Will Kiley said in a statement, adding, “House Republicans are going to defy history, and we’re going to win.”

The rising anxiety among Republicans, though, reflects a grim national environment that has triggered alarm bells up and down the ballot, with Senate Republicans suddenly forced on defense in red seats like Kansas — with control of both chambers of Congress up for grabs. Trump, too, is on a nationwide campaign swing, with stops in a more competitive part of Ohio, as well as deep-red territory like Texas, Oklahoma and Alabama.

“There’s a lot of close races, and it’s hard to make a prediction,” retiring GOP Rep. Dan Newhouse said this week of his party’s chances, but acknowledged, “Affordability is a big deal. People see the gas prices every single day.”

While Newhouse said his party has worked to address cost of living issues, he noted, “There’s just a lot of things making it tough right now for rural America — which I can speak to specifically — but for Americans all over the country.”

Many Republicans acknowledge to CNN that the souring national environment — fueled by soaring diesel prices, stubborn inflation and hardening opposition to the Iran war — are largely out of their control this late in the race. They say their strategy is now focused on how to limit Democrats to the slimmest majority possible — in a bid to make governing all but impossible for a potential House Speaker Hakeem Jeffries next year.

Johnson’s historically narrow majority — the slimmest since before World War II — has been a major headache for GOP leaders, with the Louisiana Republican unable to wield control of the floor on numerous occasions. Republicans want Jeffries to face the same problem.

Several people said their goal is to keep Jeffries’ margin to fewer than 10 seats. If that happens, one GOP strategist summarized: “What the f**k are you going to get done over there?”

Few Republicans believe it will be a total wipeout for their party in which Democrats win more than 30 seats. And some believe there is still a path to keeping their narrow majority, especially if gas prices drop significantly in the next four weeks. Party leaders are particularly confident about two incumbents in purple seats: Reps. Brian Fitzpatrick in Pennsylvania and Mike Lawler in New York, both in districts Kamala Harris won in 2024.

But there is growing anxiety from GOP members and aides about protecting parts of the country that haven’t elected Democrats to the House in decades — seats Trump won by double digits that are suddenly in play with incumbents who rarely face competitive general elections.

As of early October, Republicans are still planning to use a massive cash advantage to support their strongest incumbents, while turning up the heat on their top offensive targets, like Rep. Marcy Kaptur in Ohio’s 9th District, Rep. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez in Washington’s 3rd — and drowning Democrats in spending.

The GOP’s huge cavalry of super PACs, meanwhile, helps build a firewall around their reddest turf to avert disaster, with Trump-linked groups spending in seats once considered a reach for Democrats, but are now in play, like Colorado’s 5th District, Kentucky’s 6th District and Montana’s 1st District.

“The environment is bad but Democrats still have to win on GOP terrain,” one GOP operative said.

If House Republicans are going to pull off an upset in November, they say it would come down to the party’s massive cash advantage and its aggressive gerrymandering push.

Republicans are outspending Democrats in all of the 10 most expensive House races on advertising from now until Election Day, according to data from AdImpact. That includes multimillion-dollar advantages in Democratic-held seats like Rep. Don Davis in North Carolina’s 1st District and an open seat in Maine’s 2nd District.

Much of the GOP’s spending is concentrated in newly redrawn seats in Texas and Florida, the fates of which are still highly uncertain, especially for incumbents like GOP Rep. Monica De La Cruz in Texas. But if even a handful of those seats swing toward Republicans, it could make up for losses elsewhere.

“At the end of the day, redistricting could be the lifesaver either way — either minimizing the losses or the reason we potentially hold onto the majority,” one GOP leadership aide told CNN.

Then there are the handful of swing seats where Republicans feel more upbeat because of Democratic clashes during the primaries, which left their nominees more vulnerable. That includes California’s 22nd District, Michigan’s 7th District and that open seat in Maine — where progressives beat out establishment-preferred centrists.

Even in a challenging midterm environment, Republicans are turning to issues that they feel give them an advantage with voters — with taxes, immigration and law enforcement figuring prominently in their campaign ads.

Tax cuts on tips, overtime and Social Security delivered by the “One Big Beautiful Bill Act” were the fulfillment of a key 2024 campaign promise, and that’s been a point of emphasis. Republicans have also hammered Democrats for opposing the legislation.

“Zach Nunn voted for the largest middle class tax cut ever,” says an ad from the GOP incumbent in Iowa’s competitive 3rd District.

An analysis of AdImpact data found that about one-third of GOP ads in House races in September focused on tax policy, making it the top issue tracked by the firm.

Immigration, which ranked fourth, has been another key argument for Republicans. “Stelson wants you to pay for criminal illegal immigrants’ healthcare,” says an ad from the House GOP’s main super PAC, Congressional Leadership Fund, targeting the Democrat in Pennsylvania’s 10th District.

GOP advertisers also produced dozens of ads touting their support for law enforcement and accusing Democrats of being soft on crime. Several begin with grisly accounts of local crimes, juxtaposed with rhetoric from Democrats calling for criminal justice reform. “Attention all criminals, do we have some good news for you: Christina Hines, the liberal Ann Arbor prosecutor, is running for Congress,” says one ad airing in the competitive race for Michigan’s 10th District.

Other specific issues have also animated these key races, including Republicans’ sustained focus on transgender policies, an issue they’ve used to attack Democrats since it proved effective in the 2024 campaign. As a result, Democrats have increasingly taken to the airwaves to rebut the criticism, such as Kaptur in Ohio’s 9th District.

Republicans say the Democrats’ quick response to the transgender politics attacks show that it’s an effective issue — and believe it’s been making a dent in internal polling.

“Here’s the truth: I voted with Republicans to keep transgender ideology out of our schools because parents know what’s best for their kids, and boys should not play in girls’ sports,” Kaptur says in one ad.

This story has been updated with additional information.
