fullText:
The California Supreme Court excoriated Riverside County Sheriff Chad Bianco over his seizure of hundreds of thousands of Proposition 50 ballots earlier this year, ordering the former gubernatorial candidate to immediately hand over all remaining materials in a pair of scathing decisions Thursday.

"We hold that the seizure of the ballots was unlawful," wrote Chief Justice Patricia Guerrero. "While allegations of election improprieties are a very serious matter, our Elections Code contains numerous established mechanisms for investigating and proving misconduct that do not compromise the integrity of voted ballots — contrary to the means employed here."

California voters overwhelmingly passed Proposition 50 in a special election last fall, blessing a new congressional map that all but eliminated Republican districts in response to gerrymandering efforts in Texas and other deep-red strongholds.

Bianco, a popular MAGA personality and former Republican candidate for governor, doggedly pursued claims the Riverside County returns were fraudulent, seizing on a discrepancy between the registrar's voluntary hand tally and the official vote count to commandeer the ballots as evidence of a crime — a move the court roundly rejected.

"A criminal prosecution commences only upon the occurrence of certain events — none of which has occurred in this case — and may only be initiated by a public prosecutor," Guerrero wrote. "But even if a criminal prosecution had commenced, allowing for a court-ordered production, [the law's] plain text prohibits the removal of the ballots from the registrar's physical custody."

The ruling comes less than two weeks before Californians will start casting ballots in the race for governor and a handful of bitter congressional contests — nationally-watched elections that would be vulnerable to similar interference unless the court gave clear orders, advocates warned at oral arguments last month.

"It's bound to be repeated again," said Chad W. Dunn of the UCLA Voting Rights Project, which led the first of two related suits against Bianco.

California Atty. Gen. Rob Bonta, who brought the other suit, cheered Thursday's rulings as an important electoral safeguard.

"The Court has now made clear that this kind of defiance cannot stand," Bonta said in a statement following the twin decisions. "I encourage Californians to make their voices heard and vote early in the fast-approaching November 3 midterm elections, with the confidence of knowing that their voted ballots will never again be subject to physical seizure by rogue county sheriffs."

Bianco did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Bianco has long flirted with President Trump's election fraud conspiracy movement. Though the ballot seizures in February were widely seen as a campaign stunt, the legal theory behind them — that local lawmen can commandeer voter materials from elections officials, and that sheriffs are unanswerable to officials who outrank them, including attorneys general — belongs to a larger "constitutional sheriffs" ideology.

California's seven Supreme Court justices appeared by turns perplexed by and incredulous of those theories during oral arguments last month.

"You are walking into a very dense thicket of very specific laws that govern elections in particular and I think it's a very established cannon of interpretation that the specific trumps the general," said Associate Justice Goodwin H. Liu.

Thursday's rulings effectively short-circuited Bianco's efforts to keep the ballot probe alive.

"Bianco presumably could have used traditional investigatory tools, within the bounds of the law, to obtain other evidence of election-related crime," Guerrero wrote.

Further, the court said, Bonta's authority to stop both the seizure and the ad hoc recount was unequivocal.

"Respondents' arguments all boil down to the unsustainable view that the state's chief law enforcement officer ... must remain a mere bystander to an unprecedented sheriff's investigation of undeniable statewide significance," Guerrero wrote. "As we have explained, that is not the case."

In a footnote, justices also took a swipe at Bianco's initial effort to have the case tossed for lack of standing — a move apparently undertaken on the legal advice of an elaborate AI hallucination, reminding lawyers of their "professional duties of competence and candor."

The ballot battle emerged from a Riverside County pilot program meant to boost voter confidence — a handwritten tally that ultimately fell about 46,000 votes short of the official count, sparking claims of fraud.

The registrar of voters met with the county board of supervisors and the citizens' group behind the claim and carefully explained how the discrepancy emerged. Yet, Bianco pursued warrants to seize more than 650,000 ballots, alleging they were evidence in an investigation of wide-ranging misconduct.

When he learned of the warrants, Bonta ordered Bianco to stand down. Instead, the sheriff accelerated his plans, dispatching armed deputies from Riverside County's Special Investigations Bureau, Emergency Response Team and SWAT unit to sweep up the votes.

Later, Bianco directed his underlings to begin counting those ballots by hand — a potential felony under state law, which forbids anyone other than election officials from so much as touching a ballot container.

When Bonta again ordered him to stop, Bianco argued the attorney general had no authority to command him, later claiming in court that the law conferred only an "advise and consent" role.

Spurred by the Riverside dustup, lawmakers in Sacramento recently passed a "raft of additional legislation" to shore up ballots and empower elected officials to protect them in the future.

"It is a lot to ask of our election officials that they not only do their jobs competently but also stand ready to sue anyone who unlawfully interferes with their duties. Yet here we are," Liu wrote. "For our democracy to flourish, our elections must be conducted in accordance with the law."

fullText:
With six weeks to go until Election Day, and early voting already underway in a handful of states, the conventional wisdom is that Republicans may be in for some setbacks in the midterms.

As it defends its fragile House and Senate majorities, the GOP is fighting political history, which has traditionally seen the president's party lose congressional seats during the midterms. It's also battling high costs at the grocery stores and gas pumps tied to what polls show is an unpopular war with Iran, as well as President Donald Trump's underwater approval ratings.

But Democrats are saddled with their own issues, from an ideological civil war between the party's left wing and the establishment that has handed Republicans plenty of political ammunition, to a brand image that's nothing to brag about. Add to that the Democrats' major disadvantage as the GOP floods the airwaves with attack ads.

Here are six forces that will likely determine whether Republicans can turn back a possible blue wave and hold power in Congress.

WHO'S UP AND WHO'S DOWN IN THE LATEST FOX NEWS MIDTERM ELECTION POLLING

Six weeks until Election Day, and just as the voting begins, fuel prices keep rising, with the national average for gas nearly $4.50 per gallon and diesel topping $6.50 per gallon, according to AAA.

Public opinion polls point to the economy, including the cost of living, as the top issue for voters in this year's midterms. That means that the issue that boosted Trump and Republicans to sweeping victories in 2024 is a major liability in 2026. And the rising prices in recent weeks, fueled by renewed fighting in the war with Iran and Ukraine and attacks on Russia's diesel industry, are doing the GOP no favors.

"Gas prices were much higher under Biden than under "TRUMP." So were almost all other prices," the president argued Monday in a social media post, as he referred to former President Joe Biden.

While Trump and Republican leaders point fingers at Biden, polls indicate voters increasingly place the blame for ongoing economic and inflation pressures on the current administration.

DEMOCRACY ’26: STAY UP TO DATE WITH THE FOX NEWS ELECTION HUB

Democrats last week heavily criticized Trump and Republicans after the president argued that fuel costs were "a very inexpensive price to pay for what we’ve done," as he pointed to the attacks on Iran's nuclear facilities.

Meanwhile, the latest Fox News poll indicated that by a wide margin, the Democrats are considered the party that would better handle inflation.

But when asked about the overall economy, recent national surveys from Reuters/Ipsos and NBC News had the GOP and Democrats all knotted up on which party would better handle the issue.

"My listeners are looking for prices to come down across the board," New Hampshire-based center-right talk radio host Jack Heath told Fox News Digital.

"People elected President Trump to lower prices and improve their situation and people are looking for that improvement," Heath, host of "Good Morning NH," emphasized. "They're looking for Trump to deliver on his promises."

"I'm asking you to just pretend I'm on the ballot just one more time," the president said last week during a campaign stop in battleground North Carolina.

It's a line Trump repeatedly used earlier this month, at the GOP's first-ever midterm convention.

Facing what polls indicate is an enthusiasm gap with Democrats, the president and Republican leaders are hoping to energize the MAGA base, which doesn't always vote when Trump isn't on the ballot. While the president's approval rating in the Fox News poll stands at 39% among all voters, it remains at a sky-high 98% among self-described MAGA Republicans.

But some longtime Trump allies are starting to break with the president as they face challenging re-elections.

GOP Rep. Maria Salazar won re-election two years ago by 20 points in South Florida's 27th Congressional District. But with Trump's negative poll numbers a potential anchor around her, Salazar last week released a TV ad criticizing the Trump administration’s immigration enforcement as having "gone too far," and that "Hispanics who helped you get to the White House in 2024 feel betrayed today."

Meanwhile, on Monday two Trump allies who are in heated Senate battles - Rep. Ashley Hinson of Iowa and former Rep. Mike Rogers of Michigan, broke with the president as they a swift end to the war with Iran.

Watch whether vulnerable Republicans create more distance from the president, or move toward Trump to juice Republican turnout.

Republicans are aiming to turn what's normally a referendum on the party in power into a choice election, as they spotlight major Democratic primary victories this year by far-left and socialist candidates over more mainstream Democrats.

"In state after state, the Democrat establishment has been overthrown and replaced by crazed lunatics and radicals. They call themselves Democrat socialists, but actually, they’re communists," Trump charged at the midterm convention.

The messaging is pronounced in Michigan's crucial Senate race, where GOP nominee former Rep. Mike Rogers, as he referred to Democratic rival Abdul El-Sayed, told Fox Business this week, "We don’t want this socialism nonsense in our state, and this guy is too extreme."

12 SENATE RACES THAT WILL DETERMINE WHO CONTROLS THE CHAMBER

Polling gives a boost to the GOP's "commonsense vs. crazy" messaging.

Fifty-five percent of registered voters surveyed in the latest Fox News national poll held an unfavorable view of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), while only three in 10 saw the DSA in a positive light.

The Fox News poll was the latest national survey to show that while the DSA has gained traction among Democrats, the group and the broader socialist movement in America face significant national skepticism.

While the GOP full court press continues, in hopes of swaying undecided voters, Democrats are divided on its effectiveness.

Ty Strong, founder and president of the Moderate PAC, warned that the GOP playbook "absolutely could be effective."

But Shannon Jackson, a key consultant and advisor to progressive leader Rep. Ro Khanna of California, argued that Republicans are "reaching for things. I think the DSA issue is something they’re trying to make something, but it is not."

Meanwhile, this year's primary surge by socialist and left-wing candidates isn't helping Democrats boost their brand.

The party's favorable ratings hit historic lows in the months following the 2024 election, and the latest Fox News poll indicates Democrats are still well underwater, with 55% of voters viewing the party in an unfavorable light.

Republicans enjoy a formidable cash advantage over the Democrats, and they're using it in the final stretch leading up to Election Day.

While Democratic candidates in many key races have outraised their GOP opponents, the Republican National Committee remains far ahead of the rival Democratic National Committee when it comes to cash-on-hand.

And GOP-aligned outside groups, including the Trump-allied MAGA Inc., are opening the floodgates when it comes to ad spending, in order to try and level the playing field by overcoming the difficult political environment.

Republican groups have outspent their Democratic counterparts by more than $83 million to run spots in ten crucial Senate races since the start of September, according to figures from AdImpact, a nationally known firm that tracks ad spending.

While a financial advantage is not always decisive, strategists say it can often move the needle in a close contest. And in the 10 Senate races spotlighted by AdImpact, a onetime Democratic ad spending advantage over the summer turned into a major GOP deluge.

While much of the ad dollars dished out by Republicans are to protect vulnerable seats, the money may help as the GOP works to flip open-Democrat-held Senate seats in Michigan and New Hampshire.

Thirteen months ago, Texas passed a new congressional redistricting map, giving Trump his first major victory in his push to give Republicans a big boost heading into the midterm elections by drawing more right-leaning districts.

Fast-forward to present day, and as they fight to hold their razor-thin House majority, Republicans were the big winners, with partisan redistricting netting them potentially 10 additional right-leaning congressional seats in time for the midterms.

But redrawing the maps and winning the seats are two different things, and some election analysts caution that the fierce headwinds facing the GOP could lead to Republicans falling far short of their original expectations heading into the redistricting wars.

There are 435 seats in the House of Representatives, but the Cook Report suggests the battle for the chamber's majority could come down to just 21 districts it rates as toss-up.

The Fox News Power Rankings list 17 seats as true toss-ups.

Decades of gerrymander, including this cycle's mid-decade redistricting, has made a major impact by narrowing the House battlefield, which may limit the number of pickups by the Democrats even if a blue wave forms.

While the number of competitive House seats stays historically small, the Senate map is widening, which is a positive sign for Democrats.

Democrats are feeling the heat in open-seat contests in Michigan and New Hampshire, two must holds for them as they try to win back a Senate currently controlled 53-47 by the GOP.

But Senate showdowns in red states, including Alaska, Kansas, Nebraska, and Iowa, are now considered very competitive.

Need proof: Vice President JD Vance campaigned in Iowa and Kansas last week.

But recent polling is also giving Republicans hope they can flip the Democrat-controlled open Senate seat in blue-leaning Minnesota.

fullText:
The impeachment effort against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth posed a dilemma for Republican leaders ahead of the midterms. In the lame duck, it could be Democrats in the bind.

Hegseth is leading an unpopular war in Iran, and GOP leaders were eager to avoid an impeachment vote this month, which would have put some vulnerable Republicans in a tough spot heading into November’s elections. Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) defused the issue by punting that vote until after the elections.

But the tides are likely to turn after the election, when Republicans will be freed to weigh in on Hegseth’s fate without fear of a voter backlash, while Democrats will face a tougher choice.

Do they go charging after Hegseth full bore, to appease a liberal base demanding Pentagon accountability? Or do they tread more cautiously, to allow time for the formal investigations many Democrats say they want to see before backing something as explosive as impeachment?

Rep. Jamie Raskin (Md.), the senior Democrat on the House Judiciary Committee, which has jurisdiction over impeachment proceedings, suggested that answering those questions won’t be easy.

“I think that all impeachment articles should be sent to the Judiciary Committee, and we should scrutinize them,” Raskin, a former professor of constitutional law, said last week as Congress was leaving Washington for the long campaign recess.

“I’m not a huge fan of pop-up impeachments,” Raskin continued, “but if that’s all Speaker Johnson leaves us, then we will have to take it very seriously.”

The issue will be an early, postelection test for House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.), who has walked a delicate line under President Trump’s second term as he vies to become the first Black Speaker in U.S. history.

On one hand, Jeffries has faced pressure from the left to fight the president tooth and nail at every turn, no matter the topic. On the other, Jeffries has sought to avoid alienating more moderate voters who are the key to winning battleground districts.

His decision will become even trickier if Democrats flip control of the House, because Jeffries’s ascension to the Speakership will hinge on his ability to win 218 votes on the floor in the first week of January. That task will require the support of all Democrats, from battleground centrists who are cold to aggressive impeachments, to incoming democratic socialists who might view the vote on Hegseth’s removal as a gauge of Jeffries’s leadership credentials.

Jeffries has taken pains to balance those pressures by attacking Hegseth’s track record and calling for his firing while refusing to say if he’ll support impeachment.

“We haven’t ruled anything out when it comes to all of the tools available to us to hold people accountable, and we haven’t ruled anything in. That’s been our position. That will remain our position,” Jeffries told reporters in the Capitol last week.

“Pete Hegseth should’ve never been confirmed. This guy is the most unqualified so-called secretary of war in American history,” he added. “He’s the architect of Operation Epic Failure in Iran that has increased gas prices on everyday Americans and further burdened them economically. … It’s my view that’s the reason why [GOP leaders] pulled the resolution, because there were Republicans who can’t even defend Pete Hegseth at this point.”

The resolution in question, sponsored by Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.), features eight articles of impeachment accusing Hegseth of abuses of power related to his handling of the Iran war, a failure to protect civilians and the extrajudicial killings of alleged drug smugglers in international waters, among other charges. Massie introduced the proposal as a privileged resolution, which forces a floor vote even over the objections of GOP leaders.

Johnson evaded that vote by cutting the House calendar a day short last week. But the clock resumes when the House returns on Nov. 9, making Hegseth’s impeachment a first order of business in the lame-duck session.

Democrats have seized on Johnson’s decision, saying Republicans simply feared taking a tough vote ahead of the midterms — an attack that’s allowed them to highlight the unpopular Iran war.

“You talk to Republicans here — which I do a lot, because I’m on the Armed Services and Intel committee — a vast majority of people do not like Pete Hegseth. They think he’s incompetent, at best. They think he’s a clown and a joker at worst. … And a lot of people are somewhere in between,” said Rep. Jason Crow (D-Colo.). “They don’t want to vote on it.”

Johnson has rejected that narrative as “ridiculous,” saying he simply wanted to grant lawmakers more time to campaign.

But attacking Johnson over the process is different from throwing your weight behind impeachment. Even after the vote was delayed, Democratic leaders distanced themselves from Massie’s resolution and promoted a more deliberative process.

“The DOD mismanagement is incredibly clear, but let’s be honest. The only calls, the only discussions about impeachment in the halls of Congress this week have been from Republicans to impeach Pete Hegseth. No Democratic members were making those calls,” said Rep. Pete Aguilar (Calif.), the chair of the House Democratic Caucus.

“We believe in oversight and accountability — that is a hallmark of what this chamber should be doing,” he continued. “We will do that job. We will do it in a thoughtful way.”

Aguilar’s remarks ignored another impeachment push just before the recess, when Democratic Rep. Al Green (Texas) forced a vote to remove Trump over the killing of several civilians by immigration enforcement officers. Many Democrats were furious with Green for distracting from the party’s economic message, and every member of leadership sought to balance competing internal interests by voting “present” — a strategy that could forecast how they’ll approach the Hegseth resolution.

However, heading into that vote, at least one powerful Democrat said Massie has made “very compelling” points about the laws of war and the possibility that Hegseth violated them, which could make it tough for Democrats to do anything but support impeachment.

“He raises a bunch of profound arguments,” Raskin said, “and I’m taking it extremely seriously.”

description:

A federal appeals court ruled Monday that Missouri must use a GOP-friendly congressional redistricting plan for November’s election but put that ruling on hold for a week so the Supreme Court could review the dispute.

fullText:
A federal appeals court ruled Monday that Missouri must use a GOP-friendly congressional redistricting plan for November’s election but put that ruling on hold for a week so the Supreme Court could review the dispute.

The ruling from the US 8th Circuit Court of Appeals is the latest twist in a whiplash legal wrangling over the map of the state’s eight congressional districts, injecting another round of uncertainty, as it does not take effect immediately but rather sets up another round of appeals.

The Missouri Supreme Court previously said the 7-1 Republican-leaning map adopted by the legislature last year could not be used because of a referendum challenge brought against it under the state constitution. Instead, the court ordered election officials to use an older, 6-2 redistricting plan even though the 2025 plan had been used in the state’s primary. The US Supreme Court declined to reverse that ruling, and it then paused a federal judge’s ruling that sought to revive the 7-1 map.

The new ruling from the 8th Circuit said requiring voters to cast general election ballots on the older plan violates the US Constitution.

It relied on estimates put forward by a conservative group in the case to conclude “that more than 1.4 million Missourians could not vote for the congressional district nominees who will appear on their November 2026 general election ballot, and more than a quarter-million Missourians who voted in the August 2026 primary election cast a vote for a congressional district candidate who now cannot represent them.”

Missouri’s new map targeted the 5th Congressional District, held by Democratic Rep. Emanuel Cleaver, by breaking up its Kansas City base and stretching it into rural and Republican-leaning parts of the state.

The group that launched the referendum campaign against the GOP-leaning map noted in a statement reacting to the new ruling that “Ballots have been printed, and Missourians have already voted.”

“Thousands more will vote before this order seeks to take effect,” the statement from People Not Politicians said. “Officials should stop wasting taxpayers’ money on pointless legal action and instead focus on administering our elections.”

This story has been updated to correctly reflect the number of congressional districts in Missouri.

CNN’s Fredreka Schouten and John Fritze contributed to this report.

title: The 2026 midterms are 6 weeks away. What the latest polls say.
description:
The 2026 midterm elections are just 43 days away. All of the key primaries have been decided. With summer officially behind us, the fall campaign is now underway.
So where do things stand — nationwide — in the race to control Congress? Which party has a better chance of, you know, winning?
fullText:
The 2026 midterm elections are just 43 days away. All of the key primaries have been decided. With summer officially behind us, the fall campaign is now underway.

So where do things stand — nationwide — in the race to control Congress? Which party has a better chance of, you know, winning? To get a sense of that, it helps to zoom out … and geek out over some cold, hard data.

The usual caveats apply, of course. Polls aren't predictions; they're momentary snapshots of public opinion. Big events can, and often do, change the course of elections. And six weeks can be an eternity in politics.

Yet the stakes in November couldn't be higher, especially for President Trump, who has enjoyed complete Republican control of Congress for the first half of his second term. Flipping the House would give Democrats the power to block the president's agenda, investigate his administration and even impeach him (again); flipping the Senate would allow them to stymie his Supreme Court nominees too.

The state-by-state midterm landscape is finally taking shape — and a few clear polling trends are emerging. Here are the numbers to watch as Election Day nears.

Every pollster asks a version of the same question: If an election for U.S. Congress were held today, which party's candidate would you vote for in your district? In fact, this particular polling prompt is so pervasive, it's known as the "generic ballot" (at least among politics nerds).

You obviously can't divine the outcome of an entire midterm election from a single question that flattens 435 House contests into a binary choice between "the Democrat" and "the Republican." But the generic ballot can suggest which direction voters are heading.

History is helpful here, courtesy of the RealClear Politics polling average:

At this point in 2022 — after more than a year and a half of Democratic President Joe Biden and Democratic majorities in the House and Senate — Democrats had a narrow lead (1.3 percentage points) on the generic ballot. Six weeks later, the GOP translated its final polling lead of 3 percentage points into nine seats — enough to flip the House.

At this point in 2018 — with Trump as president and Republican majorities in the House and Senate — Democrats were leading by an average of 8 points on the generic ballot. Six weeks later, they picked up 41 seats and flipped the House.

Polarization wasn't as extreme in 2014 and 2010, the two midterms under Democratic President Barack Obama; minds weren't made up quite so early. But six weeks out, voters were starting to break against Democrats. In 2014, a final Republican polling lead of 2.4 points translated into a net gain of 13 seats in the House; in 2010, those numbers were 9.4 points and 63 seats, respectively.

So what does that mean for 2026? Historically speaking, a president's party almost always loses seats when voters return to the polls to judge his first two years in office. Sometimes, the backlash is so pervasive that the president's party loses pretty much every close-ish contest — a phenomenon known as a "wave" election.

Right now, Democrats have a wave-sized lead on the generic ballot — about 8 percentage points, on average — and it has been steadily growing over the last two weeks.

Democrats probably won't reprise 2018 and flip 41 House seats again in November, in part because red-state Republican lawmakers have recently redrawn congressional maps across the South to benefit their party in ways that blue-state Democrats have been unable to keep up with. But they only need to pick up three seats to win back the House.

National dynamics tend to define the composition of the incoming House. But Senate contests are quirkier — more state-specific and personality-driven. Democrats currently hold 47 Senate seats; they'd need 51 to control the chamber. (A 50-50 split would give Vice President JD Vance the tiebreaking vote). Polls suggest that flipping four Republican seats is possible — but Dems are also playing defense in places like Michigan, Georgia and New Hampshire. Here are the 10 races to follow:

Republican Susan Collins (incumbent)

What the latest polls say: Jackson, who replaced Graham Platner, the Democrats' previous scandal-plagued nominee, tends to lead Collins by anywhere from 2 to 8 percentage points. One recent poll shows a tie.

Republican Mike Rogers (former member of Congress)

Democrat Abdul El-Sayed (public-health epidemiologist and former Wayne County, Mich. health director)

What the latest polls say: Eight polls have been conducted over the last month. Seven of them showed El-Sayed in the lead, by anywhere from 2 to 5 percentage points.

Republican Jon Husted (incumbent)

Democrat Sherrod Brown (former senator)

What the latest polls say: Every poll conducted since July shows Brown leading Husted, with margins ranging from 4 to 8 percentage points.

Democrat Jon Ossoff (incumbent)

Republican Mike Collins (member of Congress)

What the latest polls say: Ossoff holds a solid lead over Collins, with the two most recent polls putting him ahead by 4 to 7 percentage points.

Republican Michael Whatley (former Republican National Committee chairman)

Democrat Roy Cooper (former governor)

What the latest polls say: Cooper leads by more than 8 points, on average. One poll conducted in Septemeber showed him ahead by 15.

Republican John E. Sununu (former U.S. senator)

Democrat Chris Pappas (four-term U.S. representative) 

What the latest polls say: Pappas and Sununu, who both won their Sept. 8 primaries, have traded leads in recent polls in the race to replace retiring Democratic Sen. Jeanne Shaheen. But the most recent survey, conducted from Sept. 16 to 17, showed Pappas ahead by 8.

Republican Dan Sullivan (incumbent)

Democrat Mary Peltola (former member of Congress)

What the latest polls say: Most surveys conducted since Alaska's Aug. 18 primary have given Peltola a slim lead; a mid-September AARP poll showed her ahead by 7. But the most recent sounding suggests this could be a photo finish.

Republican Ashley Hinson (member of Congress)

Democrat Josh Turek (state legislator and former Paralympic athlete)

What the latest polls say: Hinson and Turek have traded small leads in surveys released since Iowa's June 2 primaries.

Republican Ken Paxton (state attorney general)

Democrat James Talarico (state legislator)

What the latest polls say: Nearly every poll conducted over the summer has shown Talarico leading Paxton, though the margins are small — between 1 and 6 points.

Republican Pete Ricketts (incumbent and former governor)

Independent Dan Osborn (veteran and former union leader with Democratic support)

What the latest polls say: Surveys are few and far between. But the most recent results suggest Osborn could be competitive.

Advantage? Too close to call — though Democrats seem to have gained ground over the last two weeks.

To one degree or another, midterm elections are always referendums on how the president is performing. So Trump is the final piece of the puzzle.

At the moment, that's unfortunate news for Republicans on Capitol Hill and those looking to join them.

According to the data journalists at Silver Bulletin, 59% of Americans, on average, currently disapprove of how Trump is handling his job vs. 39% who approve. That puts the president's net disapproval rating at 20%.

An American Research Group poll released on Monday measured Trump's approval rating at 29% — his lowest mark ever. The same survey showed the president's disapproval rating at 68%.

Again, history can provide perspective. In mid-September 2018, Trump was about 12 points "underwater"; Republicans went on to lose 41 seats that November.

Trump is earning even lower marks on voters' top 2026 issue: the cost of living. Shortly after he returned to office, roughly equal numbers of Americans approved and disapproved of how the president was handling inflation. But today, 71% disapprove and 26% approve. That's a 45-point gap.

In comparison, Biden's approval rating on inflation was rarely underwater by more than 30 points during his presidency  — a period that coincided with the economic shocks of COVID-19 and ended with him choosing not to stand for reelection.

fullText:
Another leg up in gas prices to begin September underscores the political headwind that President Trump and Republicans face on the issue, with less than seven weeks left before the midterm elections.

The average price of US regular gasoline was $4.32 per gallon last Monday, according to the latest weekly data from the Energy Information Administration (EIA), a nearly $0.25 rise over the last two weeks.

The EIA data, which goes back to 1990, also shows that gas prices are the highest they've ever been at this stage in any recent election cycle, according to a Yahoo Finance analysis.

The second-highest price on record at this point — 49 days from an election — came in 2012 when gas cost $3.88 per gallon. The third-highest price was $3.65 in 2022. Both were election years when a Democratic administration was in power, and Republicans put a heavy focus on the issue of pump prices.

"Gas prices are at crazy levels--fire Obama!" then private citizen Donald Trump posted to social media back in 2012.

With Trump now in office, gas prices are being pushed up by a variety of factors, including both the wars in Iran and Ukraine, and they're hitting as Trump has few options to lower them due to widening disruptions in the Middle East and the Strategic Petroleum Reserve at historically low levels after months of withdrawals.

Diesel, which broke through all-time high prices earlier this month and hit another record high last Tuesday, is yet another economic headwind.

The historical data also shows that prices tend to decline in the run-up to election day — in keeping with fall trends — but this year may be an outlier.

Nonpartisan energy analysts are downplaying the chances of significant price easing in the weeks or months ahead.

"In a typical year, the consumer would see a seasonal decline in gasoline prices as refiners switched from the more expensive summer grade gasoline to the less expensive winter grade formulation," Andrew Lipow, president of Lipow Oil Associates, told Yahoo Finance.

But "this has been anything but a typical year," he said, noting that substantial price increases in gasoline and diesel could be felt across a range of consumer goods and are "wiping out the season savings that the consumer has come to expect."

GasBuddy's Patrick De Haan added in a recent blog post that the transition to cheaper winter-blend gasoline may help some, but "the scale of ongoing geopolitical escalations makes meaningful price relief unlikely in the near term."

title: Elon Musk's spending draws additional attention to Texas Senate race
description:
Musk has so far stayed out of the spotlight in the Senate race in Texas, even though he lives in the state, has based his companies Tesla and SpaceX there, and employs about 20,000 people. (Chip Somodevilla / Getty Images file)
The last time Elon Musk sank money into an election, he played a starring role in the 2025 state Supreme Court race in Wisconsin. He donned an oversized cheese hat, offered $1 million checks to voters, and he and affiliated groups poured at least $20 million into the contest.
In the end, the conservative candidate lost by 10 points in what was widely viewed as a rebuke of Musk and the Trump administration.
Now, the richest person in the world is back boosting Republican candidates in critical midterm elections, including a bruising Senate race in Texas where Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton is facing Democrat James Talarico, who had initially far outraised him and remains close in polling.
fullText:
The last time Elon Musk sank money into an election, he played a starring role in the 2025 state Supreme Court race in Wisconsin. He donned an oversized cheese hat, offered $1 million checks to voters, and he and affiliated groups poured at least $20 million into the contest.

In the end, the conservative candidate lost by 10 points in what was widely viewed as a rebuke of Musk and the Trump administration.

Now, the richest person in the world is back boosting Republican candidates in critical midterm elections, including a bruising Senate race in Texas where Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton is facing Democrat James Talarico, who had initially far outraised him and remains close in polling.

But that financial tide is quickly turning — with Musk’s help.

Unlike in Wisconsin, Musk has so far stayed out of the spotlight in Texas, even though he lives in the state, has based his companies Tesla and SpaceX there, and employs about 20,000 people. He hasn’t announced plans for any in-person events, or teased — as he did in Wisconsin — that he’d be handing out $1 million checks to voters.

Privately, Republicans say they want Musk to keep his distance. In interviews, more than half a dozen Republican strategists involved in the Texas Senate race say they hope Musk follows his 2024 model of electoral involvement, which led to a Republican sweep of the White House and Congress. Then, Musk spent more than $250 million on Donald Trump and his party.

Republicans believe Democrats will attempt to turn Musk into a boogeyman if he takes on a higher-profile role in Texas or other battlegrounds. One Republican consultant involved in the Texas Senate race said that was the perception in Wisconsin.

“He came in super late, and it was very public,” said the consultant, who, like others interviewed for this article, were granted anonymity to speak candidly. “Elon spending money became the story, which I think maybe was a mistake.”

A different Republican strategist involved in Texas campaigns said those around Musk learned from the experience.

“Did Elon bring some things to the Wisconsin race that hampered things? Probably,” the person added. “But I think they will adjust for that.”

Democrats, however, say they welcome Musk more publicly entering the fray in Texas.

“Elon, bring it. You’ve failed in Wisconsin. You’ll fail in Texas,” said Nathan Johnson, a Democrat running to replace Paxton as attorney general. “I’m not afraid of Elon bringing his political money here. All these policies favor him or people like him.”

An in-your-face Musk campaign would play into Talarico’s narrative that the real American divide isn’t left versus right but “top versus bottom,” with elites and billionaires exerting control over the working class, they say.

“James is running largely on costs and corruption,” Luke Warford, a Texas-based Democratic strategist and chair of the Travis County Democratic Party, said of Talarico. “The idea of the richest man in the world coming in late to try to buy the election and save Ken Paxton really plays into James Talarico’s argument.”

The Texas Senate race has all the makings of a contest that would attract Musk. The conservative narrative building against Talarico amplifies his past remarks in support of transgender people, including his comment that “God is nonbinary.” Talarico told Fox News he was being “provocative” and was trying to convey that one cannot use “human categories to define God.”

Musk has spoken publicly about his own transgender daughter, Vivian Jenna Wilson, saying she was “not a girl” and was figuratively “dead.” He also alleged that he had been “tricked” into authorizing trans-related medical treatment for her when she was 16. Wilson previously told NBC News that Musk was an absent father who was cruel to her as a child for being queer and feminine.

At this point, Musk’s America PAC has not said how much it will invest in Texas, but a person with knowledge of the group’s thinking indicated that as of now, the Paxton-Talarico contest was not slotted to receive more focus than other Senate or congressional races the group is investing in across the country, saying “every state and district where we are spending is a priority.”

To date, America PAC has spent nearly $5.2 million on digital ads, mail, live calls and pamphleting in Texas, but that number is expected to significantly climb.

In all, the super PAC has spent $14.7 million on congressional races, including seven Senate races and nearly three dozen House races. The group has spent the most money on the Texas Senate race, followed by nearly $3 million on Senate races in Ohio and Michigan.

National Republican groups long knew they would have to provide air cover for Paxton because of an initial fundraising disadvantage to Talarico, who had $21 million in cash on hand compared to Paxton’s $1.7 million at the end of June, according to campaign finance reports. Today, a flood of Republican money is pouring in from several sources and the balance has suddenly tipped in Paxton’s favor.

“America PAC is working in full coordination with the entire GOP apparatus and is investing in the states and districts that will decide control of the House and Senate,” America PAC spokesman Andrew Romeo said in a statement. “Our only priority is ensuring Republicans keep full control of Washington and stopping the lunatic left from bringing us back to the days of open borders, rampant crime, and woke policies.”

Paxton’s status as a scandal-plagued candidate who has been impeached and indicted — coupled with the fact he’s coming off a contentious primary against Sen. John Cornyn and much of the Republican Party establishment, aside from Trump — makes him among the most vulnerable front-line Senate Republican candidates in a state where Democrats have not won a statewide post in three decades.

After Trump’s late endorsement helped propel Paxton over Cornyn, groups like the Senate Leadership Fund, the super PAC affiliated with Senate Majority Leader John Thune, and the National Republican Senatorial Committee, were left scrambling. The election cycle budgets were, in part, built on the idea that Cornyn would not need nearly as much national fundraising help.

“Cornyn had his own fundraising machine, he could raise a lot of money on his own, so it was going to make things easier to cover other important close races,” said a Republican consultant familiar with the thought process. “I know they [Elon] are focused more on the ground game stuff. MAGA Inc. is on digital and mail. This pretty much turned out the way we thought it would. It’s an expensive endeavor and a team and multigroup effort.”

The pro-Paxton Lone Star Liberty PAC has pumped at least $15 million into TV ads that have included hitting Talarico on previous votes involving China.

So far, MAGA Inc. has spent $10 million in the state to help boost Paxton, its second-biggest single-state investment.

The group did not return a request for comment, but in an interview with NBC News last week, MAGA Inc. chief James Blair said the group had booked $10 million worth of TV ad time in Texas. Blair noted the previous disparity in spending, with Talarico and related groups pummeling Paxton on TV.

“The fact is Ken Paxton had $100 million spent against him in the primary,” Blair said. “Talarico had $0 spent against him in the primary, and that has an impact on candidate images that takes time to rectify. But the resources … have begun to be deployed now in earnest [and] will take care of that problem.”

A veteran GOP official directly involved in the race contended that the shift toward spending in Texas did not take away from other battlegrounds.

“This spending will not take away from other investments,” the official said. “This came from a collection of Texas folks very committed to making sure that seat remains Republican. They see the polling, and that James Talarico is so extreme. No one wants to see Texas turn blue.”

When asked about the onslaught of money headed toward Talarico, spokesman JT Ennis said, “Billionaire-backed dark money groups are lying about James because they’re scared of the people-powered movement we’re building to fix this broken, corrupt political system.”

fullText:
President Donald Trump’s sinking ratings threaten to drag down Republicans in November’s midterm elections, as voters blame him for high prices and a shaky economy, according to a new NBC News poll.

The president’s approval rating stands at 41% among registered voters, a second-term low in the poll, with a majority (55%) of voters saying they believe Trump’s policies have hurt the economy. That’s up from 48% in March, before the Iran war pushed up prices on gas and other goods and cemented the rising cost of living as voters’ most pressing issue.

Democrats hold a 5-point edge in the battle for control of Congress, 50%-45% — not nearly as large a lead as the 12-point advantage the party enjoyed at this point before the 2018 election, when Democrats rode an anti-Trump wave to the House majority in his first midterm as president. Despite that lead, the Democratic Party is still viewed more negatively than Trump and the GOP.

That could help Republicans, along with the fact that the fight for control of the House and especially the Senate is playing out in traditionally Republican parts of the country. Democrats would have to flip multiple states Trump carried by double digits in 2024 to win the Senate.

“We have a classic battle between these numbers and the political geography in which this campaign will be decided,” said Republican pollster Bill McInturff of Public Opinion Strategies, whose firm conducted the survey alongside Democratic firm Hart Research Associates. “And the Republicans are still standing because of the geography in which this election will be won or lost.”

Still, the poll suggests an increasingly gloomy political environment for the GOP. Longtime double-digit leads over the Democratic Party on who would better handle inflation and the economy have evaporated. More than 6 in 10 voters say the Iran war has not been worth it. Voters don’t appear to be motivated by Trump’s signature tax and spending legislation he championed last year.

Instead, Trump himself is a powerful motivating factor, but more for Democrats than for Republicans, as more voters — including nearly half of independents — say they consider their vote a signal of opposition to the president than at any other time in three decades of NBC News polling before midterm elections.

“Donald Trump has achieved his goal of making this election about him at a historic level. The problem for Trump and Republicans on the ballot in November is that he has also made history in the highest share of voters who say their vote is in opposition to Trump,” said Democratic pollster Jeff Horwitt of Hart Research Associates.

Republicans on the campaign trail are trying to shore up their standing by arguing that Democrats are too extreme to trust with congressional majorities.

But the poll indicates voters are more anxious about restraining Trump: 50% say they’re more concerned that Republicans will go too far in supporting Trump if they keep control of Congress, while 42% are more concerned Democrats will obstruct the president if they win control of Congress. Independents lean 45%-30% toward greater concern that Republicans will go too far supporting Trump.

McInturff acknowledged the challenges for the GOP posed by the political environment, even as the party’s geographic advantages keep Democrats fighting on their turf.

“The issue environment is tilting substantially towards the Democrats,” McInturff said.

A majority of voters, 56%, disapprove of Trump’s job performance, including overwhelming shares of Democrats and independents and 16% of Republicans. The share of voters who strongly approve of Trump, 25%, is the second-lowest mark recorded in the NBC News poll across Trump’s first and second terms.

The disapproval rating closely tracks the 55% who say Trump’s policies have hurt the economy, while 26% say they have helped and 18% say they have not made much of a difference. At this point in the 2018 election cycle, more voters said Trump’s policies helped the economy (41%) than hurt (26%).

And the survey suggests some of Trump’s signature economic policies are falling flat.

While Republicans are touting Trump’s signature tax cut and spending measure known as the “big, beautiful bill,” which was enacted in 2025, 42% of voters say they are less likely to support a candidate backing the measure, while 36% say they are more likely to support such a candidate.

Trump’s latest gambit — an announcement at the recent Republican convention that he wanted to issue $5,000 payments to every adult if Republicans keep control of Congress — isn’t garnering much interest. While 21% of voters say they’re more likely to back a candidate who supports Trump’s plan, 46% say they’d be less likely.

A plurality of Republicans say it would make no difference in their vote choice, while Democrats are uniformly against the idea and 45% of independents would be less likely to support a candidate in favor of the plan. Among independents, 13% say they’d be more likely to support a candidate who backs Trump’s plan.

Voters are also continuing to express opposition to the Iran war, with 57% saying they are less likely to support a candidate who supports the war, versus 24% who are more likely to support that candidate. One-third of voters say the war has been worth it, while 62% disagree.

And Democrats also have a 4-point advantage, within the poll’s margin of error, on the question of which party voters say they trust to handle the war with Iran.

Trump has continued to insert himself into the midterms, including endorsing nearly all Republicans in competitive congressional races. But 52% of voters are less likely to support a candidate endorsed by Trump, while 30% are more likely to support a Trump-backed candidate.

Clear dissatisfaction with the president opens the door for Democrats as they fight for control of Congress this fall.

Forty-three percent of registered voters say their vote for Congress is intended to signal opposition to Trump, while 27% say they plan to vote to send a signal of support for Trump and 28% say their vote won’t be a signal either way.

Among independents, almost half (46%) see their vote as a signal of opposition to Trump, while just a handful (10%) say their vote is a signal of support for the president.

Democrats have a 1-point lead when voters are asked which party they trust 

Democrats also have a 7-point edge on controlling inflation, as well as slight leads on dealing with the war in Iran and dealing with corruption — government corruption was the second-most popular choice when voters were asked to rank the most important issue facing the country, with concern about the issue heightened among members of both parties and independents.

The Democratic Party also has double-digit leads on dealing with data centers and dealing with healthcare.

Republicans still hold significant advantages over Democrats on handling crime, border security and immigration, including a 21-point lead on border security. But that is down from the 36-point edge the GOP held over Democrats on the issue in Sept. 2022, after Trump has made aggressive immigration enforcement a hallmark of his second term.

Democrats also have a narrow lead on interest in the election, as well as among party identification. But it’s not all rosy for the opposition party.

The Republican Party is viewed more positively by voters: 36% have a positive view of the GOP, while 49% view the party negatively. On the Democratic Party, voters are split 29%-50%.

Meanwhile, the Democratic Socialists of America is viewed positively by 22% of voters, as Republicans try to link other Democrats to the left-wing group, which rose in prominence following some major primary wins in the past two years.

One poll respondent — Aidan Valenzuela, a 19-year-old Texan who doesn’t affiliate with either party — told NBC News that he hasn’t plugged into the election yet and is still unsure whom he’ll vote for. But he said his father grew up during the Cold War and that he’s wary of Democrats who describe themselves as democratic socialists.

“Any relation toward socialism or communism in general gives me the ick. It’s like a buzzword that generally just makes me not want to sway in that direction,” he said.

Half of voters say they’d be less likely to vote for a candidate who “supports many of the Democratic Socialists of America’s proposed policies,” while 31% say they’d be more likely to support those kinds of candidates.

Candidates calling to abolish ICE, a big point of emphasis among progressives, draw similarly unpopular scores with voters.

That said, for all the Democratic infighting over policies like “Medicare for All,” 53% of voters say they would be more likely to support a candidate who favors the policy, while 36% said it would make them less likely to vote for that candidate.

When asked a similar question with slightly different wording to note the healthcare would be financed in part by taxes, 49% say they’d be more likely to support a candidate that backed the policy and 39% say they’d be less likely.

Horwitt, the Democratic pollster, noted that his party “remains in a terrible position as a brand nationally,” even as the poll paints a dismal picture for Trump and Republicans.

“This speaks more to deep dissatisfaction with Trump and Republicans than a ringing endorsement of Democrats,” he said. “The party in power does not have a positive story to tell on the major issues of the day: inflation, corruption and the Iran war. Voters are continuing to look for change.”

The NBC News poll surveyed 1,000 registered voters Sept. 11-15 via a mix of telephone interviews and an online survey sent via text message. The margin of error is plus or minus 3.1 percentage points.

'It will never be the same': How the Kennedy Center got stuck in a cultural quagmire
description:

fullText:
When President Donald Trump’s name was ordered removed from the Kennedy Center this spring, it seemed that an opening to move on from his reign over the performing arts center might have emerged.

“I have instructed the Department of Commerce to make all necessary arrangements with Congress to allow a full and complete transfer of this Institution, giving them the responsibility for its Operation, Maintenance, and Management,” the president wrote in a late-May Truth Social post, seemingly relinquishing the control he’d seized a year prior.

Speculation even bubbled up among some of the more than a dozen “ex-officio,” board members — who don’t get a vote but are not allied with Trump — over whether the former board chairman, billionaire philanthropist David Rubenstein, could be brought back to help restore the center’s fundraising and programming, two sources familiar with the matter told CNN. (CNN has asked Rubenstein for comment.)

But after Trump said he would remain chairman, “it kind of all squelched pretty quickly,” one of the sources said. The hope that his crusade to rename a monument dedicated to the memory of John F. Kennedy had ended turned out to be wishful thinking.

Instead, nine months from a cold December day when cranes first placed Trump’s name on the marble façade, the institution has been brought to the brink by the president still very much engaged in a fight: lights have been turned off inside, infrastructure is crumbling and protests swirl while legal battles mount.

A lawsuit brought by Democratic Rep. Joyce Beatty of Ohio, an ex-officio board member, led to a judge’s ruling that Trump’s name had to be scraped off the building and that the board could not shut down the facility altogether.

Trump has only ratcheted up his threats to tear down the building in response to the legal setbacks: The president was seen with a poster this week through the window of Air Force One that appeared to read “Kennedy Center DEMOLISHED.” Though the federal judge has since ordered a 30-day notice be given before any major change happens, it’s not at all clear where things go from here.

Late Friday night, the administration argued in court that the Kennedy Center must close for two years, asking the federal judge in the case to allow it so that the “dangerously dilapidated and decrepit” building can be renovated.

On the same day, over a dozen Kennedy Center employees were laid off, including its lead spokesperson, according to two sources familiar with the matter — gutting an already skeleton staff. The Kennedy Center declined to comment on the cuts.

Trump has said previous leadership is to blame for the dire financial situation. During a contentious board call this week, he also blamed Beatty for bringing litigation that, he said, has contributed to the center’s downfall.

While the president and his allies on the board argue his name needs to be re-affixed to the building to revive fundraising, current and former officials, performers and industry officials say it is precisely Trump’s involvement that alienated the center’s donors and prompted scores of artists to cancel their performances.

“The Broadway productions will not come back, the artists will not come back,” said a source familiar with discussions about programming. “None of those donors will come back as long as Donald J Trump is the chairman.”

Current and former Kennedy Center officials, musicians, artists and other performers with ties to the center suggest that Trump’s takeover has added a permanent imprint on the Kennedy Center, whether or not his name ultimately ends up on the building.

“There are wonderful theaters throughout this country, and they are certainly part of the cultural ecology,” said LaRue Allen, president and executive director of the Martha Graham Dance Company, which has a 50-year history with the institution. “But the Kennedy Center — it is our nation’s capital. It is our national showcase.”

Another Kennedy Center source who recently left said simply: “It will never be the same.”

CNN has asked the White House for comment.

Trump’s focus on the Kennedy Center is emblematic of a notable shift from his first administration to a second one that has targeted arts, cultural and educational pillars across the country, in addition to Trump’s unrelenting desire to remake the nation’s capital to his liking.

In his first term, Trump mostly avoided the venue, skipping the Kennedy Center Honors after awardees threatened to boycott the event if he attended. The White House even said in a 2017 statement that the president and First Lady Melania Trump were not participating “to allow the honorees to celebrate without any political distraction.”

And when the Kennedy Center initially received $25 million in funding in a March 2020 Covid stimulus package, Trump defended the aid, saying: “The Kennedy Center, they do a beautiful job, an incredible job.”

Nine months later, however, he singled out a $40 million line-item for the center while criticizing a subsequent December 2020 Covid aid bill — a foreshadowing of his future disaffection.

“At my direction, we are going to make the Kennedy Center in Washington D.C., GREAT AGAIN,” Trump wrote on Truth Social in February 2025.

Trump said he had fired Rubenstein as chairman of the board as well as board trustees “who do not share our Vision for a Golden Age in Arts and Culture.”

The takeover became the first domino in a cascade of Trump moves to remake the nation’s capital, including the demolition of the East Wing of the White House, the closure and remodeling of the busiest public golf course in Washington, DC, and his ongoing efforts to build a 250-foot triumphal arch near Arlington National Cemetery — projects all still being fought over in court.

Though Trump has widely criticized cultural institutions and museums, he’s been able to exert only so much control over them, primarily by reducing their federal funding. The federal government has gutted the agencies that fund the arts, including the National Endowment for the Arts and National Endowment for the Humanities, and denied and rescinded tens of millions of dollars in grants to organizations that don’t align with the president’s values.

But the Kennedy Center is one of the few cultural institutions where the president has been able to flex more of his power by seizing control of the board. He has similarly tried to bring the federally funded Smithsonian Institution to heel, with more uneven results.

A week after Trump’s board takeover, the president was named as its chairman, and he installed longtime loyalist Richard Grenell as executive director.

“So we took over the Kennedy Center,” Trump told reporters. “I’m going to be chairman of it, and we’re going to make sure that it’s good and it’s not going to be woke. There’s no more woke in this country.”

His new role prompted several cancellations, including most notably the Broadway show “Hamilton.”

Leading up to the center’s Kennedy Center Honors in December 2025, which Trump himself was hosting, the president began referring to the building as the “Trump Kennedy Center.”

On December 18, 2025, the board made that declaration official by voting to rename the facility the “The Donald J. Trump and The John F. Kennedy Memorial Center for the Performing Arts,” saying that the change honored Trump’s work at the center after taking over.

One day later, new signage was installed to add Trump’s name to the building’s façade.

The legal battle and wave of cancellations that has ensued present particular challenges for an institution that makes part of its budget from ticket sales.

Operating as a non-profit, the Kennedy Center received roughly $37 million from Congress in the last fiscal year, according to the latest appropriations legislation signed into law. But the bulk of its revenue comes from programming and private donations. In fiscal year 2024, during the Biden administration, the Kennedy Center reported $307 million in revenues, according to documents filed with the IRS.

Last year, Grenell sought to revamp the center’s calendar to include, in his words, more family-friendly programming. He brought in “Dog Man: The Musical,” based on the popular kids’ graphic novel series, at the recommendation of second lady Usha Vance.

At the same time, the center became a place to host events that lean in to Trumpian ties, including the premiere of the documentary “Melania,” a Charlie Kirk memorial and the FIFA World Cup draw (where the organization gave Trump a peace prize).

But after Trump’s name was added to the building, a wave of performers pulled out, and ticket sales sagged. Multiple sources told CNN earlier this year that attendance at the Kennedy Center had been so low that for months it had to “paper the house” — a theater term that means to fill seats by offering free or discounted tickets.

“There was a haze of despair around the performances. Nobody was showing up to performances,” Carlos Simon, the Kennedy Center composer-in-residence since 2021, told CNN.

Simon, who is in the last year of his residence, noted that the National Symphony Orchestra is now playing at other venues in Washington. He said he’s stayed in his role at the Kennedy Center “for the morale of the folks who were still there trying to do the good work of presenting music.”

“I feel really bad that it’s become this political tool or pawn, but music still has to go on,” he said.

Amid the cancellations, Trump announced in February that the Kennedy Center would close for two years on July 4 to allow for renovations — a move critics suspected was to being made more to provide cover for the shrinking pool of patrons than because of the need for such a dramatic closure.

The Kennedy Center also received an influx of funding last year thanks to Trump’s “One Big Beautiful Bill,” which contained $257 million for the center to pursue “necessary expenses for capital repair, restoration, maintenance backlog, and security structures.”

Yet the board has argued only Trump’s help can muster the funds to renovate the building — and Trump has made clear his help will only come with naming rights.

In the meantime, Matt Floca, Grenell’s successor as executive director, this week told the judge in the Beatty case that the center needs to temporarily close due to safety concerns.

Even if the building survives, officials say getting the center’s programming to return — particularly Broadway shows — would still take months if not several years.

That is under the assumption, of course, that performances would be willing to return, said the source involved in the center’s programming.

“If we started now in terms of engaging with property companies, going back and forth and getting a deal made, we could have Broadway tours back at the Kennedy Center by the basically middle of ‘27 into ’28,” the source said. “That’s how long it takes for all these pieces to be put in place.”

CNN’s Katelyn Polantz contributed to this report.

title: Newsom signs California election safeguards aimed at Trump administration
description:
An election worker puts ballots in a counting machine at the Los Angeles County Ballot Processing Center on June 3 in City of Industry. Gov. Gavin Newsom has signed bills to protect California's elections process from interference and increase transparency in campaigns. (Kayla Bartkowski/Los Angeles Times)
Gov. Gavin Newsom on Saturday signed legislation to increase security for the state’s voting systems and protect Californians’ ability to cast ballots in an effort to guard against potential interference in the Nov.
fullText:
Gov. Gavin Newsom on Saturday signed legislation to increase security for the state's voting systems and protect Californians' ability to cast ballots in an effort to guard against potential interference in the Nov. 3 election, including by the Trump administration.

Newsom pointed to the Trump administration's recent effort to restrict mail-in voting through the U.S. Postal Service, which was struck down by the U.S. Supreme Court, and the presence of federal monitors at California polls last year as evidence that Trump "will continue his efforts to interfere with the November election."

"Donald Trump won't stop until he can exert dictatorial control over your free vote and disenfranchise millions of people this November. California will stop him at every opportunity," Newsom said in a statement. "We have no bigger task than fighting to protect the right to vote from interference and meddling — the future of democracy is on the line. These bills today build upon the wall California has built to safeguard our electoral process."

The governor signed the package of bills at the Japanese American National Museum in Little Tokyo, where a year earlier federal agents gathered outside a political rally he was hosting. Then-Border Patrol Sector Chief Gregory Bovino, who had been leading the immigration operations in California, was among those outside the event, joined by agents in helmets, camouflage, masks and holding guns. Newsom described their presence as political intimidation.

One bill Newsom signed Saturday cites efforts to "weaponize law enforcement authority for political purposes," including Republican "Sheriff Chad Bianco's seizure of ballots in Riverside County," and the election monitors sent by the U.S. Justice Department to polling sites in five counties during a 2025 special election on redistricting.

Such moves "have given rise to unprecedented concerns about law enforcement interference" in elections and "[demonstrate] that these threats are not merely hypothetical," the bill by state Sen. Tom Umberg (D-Santa Ana) reads.

The law, Senate Bill 884, which takes effect immediately, requires counties to open ballot drop-off locations 30 days before an election — two days earlier than usual — and allows counties to ban electioneering, or trying to influence voters' decisions, within up to 200 feet of polling sites. It also bans police from making arrests near voting locations except for crimes against people, property, or disrupting the voting process.

Atty. Gen. Rob Bonta and Secretary of State Shirley Weber, who oversees state elections, praised the bill signings and said they stood ready to defend Californians' right to vote.

"No one should doubt the degree of our resolve in protecting our democracy," Weber said. "This legislative package ensures that California voters will not be silenced or intimidated."

Bianco, a GOP candidate for governor who placed fourth in the primary, drew swift condemnation and legal challenges this spring after he ordered deputies to seize more than 650,000 ballots from the Riverside County elections office. Voting rights groups and Bonta challenged the move, which is being decided by the California Supreme Court.

Bianco carted off truckloads of ballots from the Riverside County Registrar of Voters in February after securing a warrant based on claims that the office allowed fraudulent votes in the special election to redraw California's congressional districts under Proposition 50 in 2025.

Earlier this year, Newsom signed a bill preventing local and federal law enforcement agencies from taking ballots without a warrant.

On Saturday the Democratic governor signed a bill making it a felony to seize or order the seizure of ballots, election records or voting machines. Future seizures could be punishable by up to four years in prison.

"The federal administration and those seeking to spread lies about our democracy continue to call for interference in elections in ways we have never seen before in this country," Assemblymember Gail Pellerin (D-Santa Cruz), the bill's author and a former longtime county elections chief, said last month. "AB 282 helps ensure that every lawfully cast vote can be counted, and that the will of the voters of every political party will be respected."

Republican lawmakers argued in previous hearings that the bill is unnecessary because it is already a crime to steal ballots.

Another bill, Senate Bill 259, makes it a crime to interfere with a mail ballot on the way to or from a voter or order the seizure of ballots that are in transit to a local elections office.

Newsom signed Assembly Bill 1664, which requires elections officials to notify the attorney general and secretary of state immediately upon learning of any warrants, subpoenas or law enforcement investigations involving election records or voting equipment.

Newsom also signed bills to boost protections under the California Voting Rights Act, including an explicit ban on voter suppression and expanded access to election materials in languages other than English.

The governor also signed legislation to require more transparency from social media influencers who are paid by political campaigns. The measure, Assembly Bill 1130, came in the wake of a controversy in the June primary election when social media influencers took on a more visible role in the campaigns.

Candidates including Democratic billionaire Tom Steyer paid thousands of dollars to influencers who posted videos endorsing Steyer or talking about him in a positive light. These videos did not always disclose that influencers were paid by a candidate's campaign.

A. Times and beyond in your inbox six days a week.

This story originally appeared in Los Angeles Times.

title: Voting groups sound alarm on funding cuts that they say could affect midterm turnout
description:
