title: Campaigners told to respect rivals as local election abuse rises
description: A survey suggests more than half of candidates in the May 2026 polls in England faced harassment or intimidation.
fullText:
Political parties should require members to respect one another during elections, the Electoral Commission has said after finding rising levels of abuse.

More than half of candidates in the May 2026 English local and mayoral polls experienced a problem with harassment or intimidation, the highest level over the last four years, according to its survey of 25,000 who stood.

A report published on Monday said such issues were most likely to affect women, people from ethnic minority backgrounds and those with a disability.

The watchdog is calling on political parties to make clear in their own rules that members "must respect other campaigners", with potential disciplinary action if they do not.

The report also recommended requiring social media companies to improve protections for electoral candidates online, including rapidly removing abusive content and identifying perpetrators.

Inappropriate contact through social media was the most frequently experienced scenario of harassment or abuse for local candidates, the survey found, with disinformation through generative AI also flagged as an issue.

One candidate told the survey their daughter had "called me from school crying" because she had seen posts online branding them "racist, fascist and Nazi".

Another candidate reported being screamed at with death threats while leafleting on doorsteps, but could not run away because of their disability.

Reform UK and Labour candidates were more than twice as likely as Conservatives and Liberal Democrats to say they had experienced such issues in the May 2026 elections in England, with the Greens and independents between both groups.

Some 79% of female respondents reported avoiding the campaign trail on their own at least once, compared to just under half of male counterparts. One female candidate said they felt the need to bring their husband with them.

And a third of respondents overall considered not standing for election because of harassment, intimidation or concerns about future abuse.

Only 15% of those surveyed had reported such experiences to the police.

"These elections demonstrate the growing threats posed to democracy," the Electoral Commission's chief executive Vijay Rangarajan said.

He added: "Without improvements to candidate safety, there is a significant risk that people will be put off standing in future elections."

title: McConnell returns to the Senate for the first time since his June hospitalization
description: Republican Sen. Mitch McConnell of Kentucky returned to the Senate to vote on Monday for the first time in three months, looking noticeably more frail after he was hospitalized for a June fall in his ...
fullText:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Republican Sen. Mitch McConnell of Kentucky returned to the Senate to vote on Monday for the first time in three months, looking noticeably more frail after he was hospitalized for a June fall in his home.

McConnell's lengthy absence from the Senate generated a flood of criticism and online speculation, as he initially remained quiet for weeks about his condition. The 84-year-old senator eventually disclosed a month later that he had been "briefly unconscious" due to the fall and had also been treated for mild pneumonia in the hospital.

He briefly addressed reporters Monday from a wheelchair outside the Senate chamber, smiling but speaking slowly and with some difficulty. McConnell joked that he wasn't sure how many reporters would be there after dodging so many questions during his almost two decades as leader.

He said he was back in the Senate to work on a pending farm bill and because he has an ongoing interest in NATO and "backing up our good friends who are totally in the fight against the Russians."

Reporters and photographers were told by Senate staff not to take video of his remarks in the second-floor hallway, even though video is often permitted in that area. Still images were allowed.

McConnell, who holds the distinction of being the longest-serving Senate leader, is in his final months of his four decades in office. He is retiring at the end of January after one of the most consequential careers in modern politics.

Republicans have nominated U.S. Rep. Andy Barr to replace him, while Democrats have nominated former state lawmaker Charles Booker. McConnell has said he is determined to finish out his term.

In a statement issued before his remarks, McConnell made clear that he may still miss some votes due to his health issues.

He said that he is "still not quite back to 100%, but I've assured Leader (John) Thune that, as I continue with physical therapy on the advice of my doctors, I will do my best to be present for tough votes when our Conference needs me."

"My recovery has been a long and often frustrating process, and the lingering effects of childhood polio haven't made it any easier," McConnell said in the statement.

The senator's extended leave highlighted increasing public concern about the age of lawmakers and their capacity to carry out their duties. Speculation about his condition grew so intense at one point that Kentucky's Democratic Gov. Andy Beshear took the extraordinary step of issuing a public letter asking McConnell to update the public in a "transparent manner."

McConnell's absence was also felt over the summer as Republicans were unable to advance a farm bill out of committee. His return could give GOP leaders a needed vote as they try to advance legislation on cryptocurrency regulation and college sports.

McConnell had polio in his early childhood and has long acknowledged difficulty as an adult in walking and climbing stairs.

A statement from the Capitol physician that was included with McConnell's July release said that the senator has "experienced several falls through the year" due to his "post-polio condition." The office said his physical therapy was aimed at reducing the risk of him falling again.

"A comprehensive evaluation by a multidisciplinary team determined that he had no fractures, cardiac abnormalities, stroke, tumor, or hemorrhage," the physician's office said.

McConnell was first elected to the Senate in 1984 and was the Republican leader from 2007 until last year, serving as both majority and minority leader during that period.

Toward the end of his time as leader and in the last two years as a rank and file senator, McConnell's health has visibly declined.

He was hospitalized with a concussion in March 2023 and missed several weeks of work after falling in a Washington hotel. He twice froze up during news conferences after he returned, staring vacantly ahead before colleagues and staff. A year later, he fell and sprained his wrist while walking out of a GOP luncheon.

title: Opinion - Trump’s radical plan is to make the postal service an election gatekeeper
description: The potential to interfere with voters' ability to vote by mail is not a bug but a feature of a system designed to restrict a practice that Democrats have used more often than Republicans in recent el...
fullText:
The Trump administration has filed its third emergency appeal to the U.S. Supreme Court, asking to lift a district court injunction that blocked President Trump's U.S. Postal Service regulations imposing strict formatting and data-submission requirements on states' mail-in ballots. A whistleblower has warned that these regulations could cause many ballots to arrive late or not at all ahead of the November midterm elections.

Plaintiffs have argued that these requirements violate the constitutional provisions that restrict election administration to the states and Congress, with no role for the executive. Equally important, and overlooked, is that the administration's scarcely disguised partisan regulations violate a nearly 60-year American tradition of insulating the postal service from politics.

The potential to interfere with voters' ability to vote by mail is not a bug but a feature of a system designed to restrict a practice that Democrats have used more often than Republicans in recent elections.

Trump has made no secret of his longstanding hostility to voting by mail and objective of controlling voting nationally. "Republicans should fight very hard when it comes to statewide mail-in voting," he declared in 2020, because "for whatever reason, [it] doesn't work out well for Republicans." This year, in February, he said, "The Republicans should say, 'We want to take over.' … The Republicans ought to nationalize the voting."

His administration now officially describes its sweeping new postal service restrictions on mail ballots as election-integrity measures, not partisan ones. However, it has provided no proof of the alleged widespread fraud that the regulations would allegedly deter.

The rule doesn't just put occasional errors at risk. It is designed so that a single failure can void an entire jurisdiction's mailing. Even before finalizing the rule, internal postal service officials warned that if even one ballot's barcode in a bulk mailing fails to scan properly during verification, this policy would reject and return the entire batch.

Thus, disrupting an election doesn't require any bad actor at the local level; it only requires ordinary human error, which is guaranteed at scale, colliding with zero tolerance. The regulations would likely upend voting in the eight states where voting is conducted almost entirely by mail, like Washington and Oregon. Seven of these states, with the exception of Utah, lean Democratic.

Washington, which automatically mails ballots to more than 5 million registered voters, says compliance could require destroying and replacing more than 5 million envelopes already printed for November. It would mean fundamentally reworking procedures only weeks before voting begins. The errors that would surely arise in such a rushed process could jeopardize the entire election process of mail-in states.

Similar disruptions would also occur in states like Arizona that rely heavily but not strictly on mail-in voting. In Maricopa County, Ariz., which mails more than 2 million ballots in its initial run, a single misprinted barcode could delay the delivery of every ballot to every voter in the county.

In addition, the Postmaster General has admitted that the U.S. Postal Service will withhold delivery from any state that refuses to hand over its voter manifest. The rule therefore gives partisan opponents of mail-in voting two independent levers, one technical and one administrative, capable of stopping ballots before they reach voters.

The postal apparatus itself embodies a civic lineage older than the Constitution. In 1775, guided by Benjamin Franklin, the first Postmaster General, the Second Continental Congress established the postal service. And as with today's mail-in voting process, the early postal service facilitated democracy.

The mail served as an egalitarian highway of democratic debate, intended to distribute independent newspapers and correspondence without royal or partisan interference. The U.S. Postal Service was designed to serve as a neutral common carrier, not an executive gatekeeper or a roving board of canvassers.

"The country may not even have come into existence but for the postal service," said historian Stephen Allen Kochersperger. Through the material it disseminated, "people were reading, getting ideas of what it would be like to be an independent country."

In the late 20th century, reformers from both parties worried that partisan politics had infected the postal service. With overwhelming bipartisan support, Congress enacted the landmark Postal Reorganization Act of 1970. A central purpose was to insulate the mail from presidential and partisan political control. Upon signing the bill, President Nixon noted that his Democratic and Republican postmasters general agreed on one point: "There is no Republican way or Democratic way to deliver the mail. There is only the right way."

The act converted the postal service into an independent public corporation with a bipartisan Board of Governors — no more than five of the nine members can belong to the same party — and gave that board, not the president, the power to appoint and remove the postmaster general. By asking the Supreme Court to lift the Boston court's injunction, the administration seeks to invert the purpose of the postal service, turning an independent carrier into an instrument of executive election policing for partisan gain.

Benjamin Franklin would be turning in his grave.

Allan J. Lichtman is Distinguished Professor of History at American University, co-host of "Lichtman Live," and author of 15 books, most recently "Great American Presidents: The Twelve Who Transformed the Nation."

title: Vote against assisted dying 'cruel and inhumane'
description: Terminally ill people in the West Country say they will continue to campaign for assisted dying.
fullText:
A woman living with terminal cancer has called the decision not to legalise assisted dying "unfair, cruel and inhumane".

Nadine Thomas, from Dursley in Gloucestershire, hoped the vote, which went before MPs in Parliament last week, would enable her to choose what to do as her bone cancer progresses and treatment stops working.

The Terminally Ill Adults (End of Life) Bill would have allowed terminally ill people in England and Wales to legally end their own lives. The bill stipulated that any approval would be subject to strict safeguards, but opponents argued they were insufficient.

MPs voted 286 to 270 against it on Friday. It now cannot be reconsidered until at least the next parliament.

Nadine Thomas has campaigned in favour of the bill for the last two years so she and other terminally ill people could be "given the same consideration and dignity" as animals at the end of their lives.

"We're not worried about dying, we know we're going to die. It's how we die - we want to do it with dignity on our own terms - and for me now the chances of that happening are pretty slim," she said.

"We are expected to suffer to our very last dying breath which is unfair, it's cruel, it's inhumane."

Jenny Carruthers, from Bath in Somerset, said the result of the vote was "absolutely crushing".

She previously cared for her partner, who died of cancer in 2013.

Now living with terminal bone cancer herself, Carruthers said she wanted to have the choice to end her life at home on her terms and would continue to campaign for change.

"It's very tiring, physically and emotionally over the whole year and listening to the campaign and constantly being blocked by something that feels very unjust is a hard thing to carry," she said.

"The effect of the illnesses on our bodies just means that its harder, it's physically harder to stand there, it's physically harder to get there and to summon the courage."

The bill was originally voted for by MPs 17 months ago, but it was back in parliament this year after it stalled in the House of Lords.

MPs were given a free vote which meant they did not have to follow party lines.

This time 87 MPs did not vote - including 56 from Labour.

Gideon Amos, the Liberal Democrat MP for Taunton and Wellington, was among those who voted against assisted dying because he believed it would have impacted the freedoms of disabled and vulnerable people.

"I was fundamentally concerned that if people were to be offered assisted dying without the option of proper mental health care or palliative care then that would not be a real choice," he said.

Amos added that he feared dying people would take the option to end their lives "because they feel a burden".

Instead, he said he would like to see more support for hospice and palliative care.

title: Election chaos in this red state just got even stranger for Republicans after Supreme Court ruling
description: The Supreme Court blocked Missouri's new congressional map, forcing the state to use 2022 boundaries that favor Emanuel Cleaver's Kansas City district.
fullText:
Republicans suffered a fresh blow in Missouri after the Supreme Court blocked a congressional map that could have helped the GOP gain another House seat in November.

The ruling, handed down last week, means Missouri will use its 2022 congressional map instead of the new boundaries backed by President Donald Trump and Missouri Republicans.

Missouri held its August primary under the new map, meaning candidates won their party nominations based on one set of district boundaries. But those boundaries will change before the November election, when Missouri is expected to return to its 2022 map.

Trump Dangles $5,000 Checks As Debt Surges — But Only If Gop Can Clear Major Midterm Hurdle

Typically, states redraw their congressional and state legislative districts once every decade after the Census to account for population changes and ensure that each district has roughly the same number of residents.

The new map would have shifted parts of Democratic Rep. Emanuel Cleaver's Kansas City district into more Republican-leaning areas, making the seat more competitive.

Republicans hoped the changes would help them win seven of Missouri's eight House seats in the November midterm elections. The GOP currently holds six of the state's eight seats, while Democrats hold two.

Missouri must now use the 2022 map, which keeps Cleaver's district more favorable to Democrats.

The Supreme Court's decision came after more than a year of legal battles over which congressional map Missouri should use.

Missouri held its August primary under the new map, but the state will use its 2022 district boundaries for the November general election. That means some voters could be assigned to a different congressional district in November than the one in which they voted during the primary.

The change could affect more than 1 million voters, or nearly one-fourth of Missouri's electorate, according to an Associated Press estimate.

The conflicting court orders have added to the confusion, with the November election just weeks away. Candidates and election officials must now adjust to the 2022 boundaries.

Missouri High Court Blocks Gop-backed Congressional Maps Ahead Of Midterms; Trump Blasts 'Ridiculous' Ruling

The Supreme Court did not explain its reasoning in the brief order.

The White House did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

title: House Speaker Mike Johnson says Trump's $5,000 'dividend' needs congressional approval
description: President Donald Trump's proposal to send $5,000 to every American adult if his Republican Party maintains control of the House and Senate in the November election needs congressional approval, House ...
fullText:
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump's proposal to send $5,000 to every American adult if his Republican Party maintains control of the House and Senate in the November election needs congressional approval, House Speaker Mike Johnson said Sunday, while pledging to try to make it happen.

Trump made the unusual pitch at the party's midterm convention in Dallas last week, promising a "Trump Dividend" if voters keep the GOP in power on Capitol Hill. The president later told CBS News Texas that he did not think Congress would need to authorize the payments, though he did not specify how he could spend more than $1 trillion without lawmakers' authorization.

But Johnson, R-La., said congressional approval is needed. "I would assume, yes, he'd need Congress to act, and that's a creative idea," he said.

A few hours later, Trump said he would deliver on his promise. "The 5,000's going to happen, 100%," he told reporters before boarding Air Force One in Ireland, where he attended a pro golf tournament at his resort.

Johnson, meanwhile, said he would work to get Trump's proposal through Congress despite a small Republican margin.

"He's the big idea's president. We're going to try to implement everything we can," he said. "I commit that Congress will work through it and find consensus on that like they have to do everything else."

The dubious election-year gambit could cost more than $1 trillion, putting further strains on the country's nearly $1.8 trillion annual budget deficit and exacerbating concerns of inflation. The economy is confronted by persistent inflation and increasing interest rates, a tough combination for governing Republicans as they seek to hold on to control of Congress.

The president argues that payments would be possible because of the strong economy, but consumer sentiment is weak as gasoline prices rise because of the war with Iran and wages struggle to keep pace with inflation.

Trump told reporters earlier Sunday that the payments would be "easy enough" because the United States has a strong economy.

"We can easily handle that because we're taking in so much money," he said. "We've never done better."

Just one-third of U.S. adults approve of how Trump is handling the presidency, according to a July poll from The Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research. That compares with 37% in June and 42% who approved of his work when he took office. Majorities also disapprove of his handling of the economy and immigration, issues that were central to Trump's election in 2024.

On Sunday, Trump said the gas price will "drop like a rock" but indicated no deal any time soon with Iran to end the conflicts and reopen the Strait of Hormuz.

Johnson appeared on CNN's "State of the Union" and NBC's "Meet the Press."

title: The AfD won a shock election in Germany. Elon Musk was thrilled
description:
The billionaire and the party have developed a symbiotic relationship to spread their far-right views both in Germany and the US
The Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) party rattled European politics this week after a convincing victory in a German state election, which placed it only a few seats away from forming the country’s first state-level far right government since the second world war.
Elon Musk was thrilled.
 Continue reading...
fullText:
The billionaire and the party have developed a symbiotic relationship to spread their far-right views both in Germany and the US

The Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) party rattled European politics this week after a convincing victory in a German state election, which placed it only a few seats away from forming the country’s first state-level far right government since the second world war.

“Gut gemacht!” Musk posted on X a week ago, using the German phrase for “well done” as he congratulated AfD party leader, Alice Weidel. It was one of at least a dozen posts the Tesla and SpaceX CEO made about the AfD following the result.

The AfD reciprocated Musk’s praise, with the party’s Saxony-Anhalt leader, Ulrich Siegmund, thanking the tech mogul for his support. Siegmund, who wants German schools to focus less on responsibility for the second world war and whose top staffers include four former members of a banned neo-Nazi youth group, called Musk a “visionary”.

Musk has become a central figure in the global far-right in recent years, using his support and influence to back anti-immigrant activists, illiberal leaders and nativist parties. Along with a preoccupation with race in the UK, much of that attention has been focused on the AfD, and the major results in the Saxony-Anhalt election, and Musk’s jubilation at their win, have revived scrutiny of his connections to it.

Musk’s ties to the AfD and German far-right predate the Saxony-Anhalt vote and coincide with the billionaire’s own public rightward drift. His views on immigration, politics and race, which he expresses relentlessly on X, have over the years become indistinguishable from many AfD policies. In boosting the AfD and receiving their adulation in return, Musk and the party have developed a symbiotic relationship to spread their far-right views both in Germany and the US.

As Musk became more involved in politics in 2024, backing Donald Trump’s reelection with over $100m of his own money, he formed alliances with several other international far-right leaders who hold anti-immigration views and antipathy for democratic institutions.

Musk has appeared onstage with Argentina’s chainsaw-wielding Javier Milei, presented an award to Italy’s ultraconservative prime minister, Giorgia Meloni, then attacked Italian judges ruling on migrant rights and gave a livestreamed speech at UK anti-Islam activist Tommy Robinson’s rally where Musk claimed immigration was causing “the destruction of Britain”.

Musk also connected with Naomi Seibt, a German climate crisis skeptic and anti-immigration activist who frequently posts on X and was 24 years old at the time. Musk began personally messaging her after seeing her posts, Seibt told reporter Paul Ronzheimer of Axel Springer’s Global Reporters Network, and she promoted the AfD to him in their chats.

In late 2024, Musk wrote an opinion column for the German outlet Die Welt expressing his own support for the AfD. Musk’s op-ed claimed that Germany was on the brink of “economic and cultural collapse” that could only be solved by the AfD, which he called “the last spark of hope” for the country. He also argued that the party wasn’t extreme, giving the example that its leader Weidel has a same-sex partner who is from Sri Lanka.

“Does that sound like Hitler to you?” Musk wrote.

As Musk took a prominent role in the second Trump administration at the beginning of 2025, he used his platform and newfound political power to further boost the AfD. In early January of that year, Musk hosted a livestream for Weidel that researchers found gave her a huge boost on the platform as well as translated to a jump in German-language media coverage.

“Musk did in fact have an agenda-setting effect on traditional media in Germany,” said Jan Rau, a researcher at Research Institute Social Cohesion and Leibniz-Institute for Media Research. “You could very clearly see it. There was a huge spike of attention from traditional media for Weidel in that moment, and a lot of this attention was actually connected with Musk.”

Weeks after hosting the livestream with Weidel, Musk also appeared via livestream at an AfD rally. Only days after causing an uproar for delivering fascist-style salutes at a Trump inauguration rally, Musk told the AfD crowd in Germany that there was “too much focus on past guilt, and we need to move beyond that”. His remarks drew condemnations from Jewish leaders and accusations that he was attempting to normalize the far-right.

Musk’s close proximity to Trump and prominent role in the White House following the 2024 election magnified his political power, as well as fears from foreign governments that he was interfering in their national affairs.

After acquiring Twitter in 2022, Musk made several changes that helped boost the divisive, far-right politics of parties like the AfD. He reinstated previously banned far-right accounts, such as pro-AfD, anti-immigration Austrian activist Martin Sellner – who has taken credit for mainstreaming nativist “remigration” policies – and often promoted international right wing accounts through reposts.

“The changes Musk made to the platform has made it much easier for far-right communication,” Rau said. “That’s helpful for the AfD in many ways.”

But researchers including Rau also argue that the rightwing bubble Musk has created on X has its limits. Only around 5% of Germans use X to find news, according to a 2026 Reuters Institute survey, and many mainstream figures in the country have publicly given up on using the platform. While some of Musk’s backing of the AfD crossed over to mainstream attention, much of it in recent months has been confined to his captive audience on X.

Today, Musk is deeply unpopular in Germany, with a YouGov poll last year finding that only 19% of the country had a favorable view of the multibillionaire. Fewer still, only 13%, viewed his attempts to influence German politics acceptable. Even within the AfD, Musk is not an entirely welcome presence.

“Musk’s boosting, in some quarters, is not particularly helpful,” said Oliver Marsh, an independent researcher formerly at the nonprofit Algorithm Watch. “A lot of the party are traditional German nationalists and don’t really approve of an American billionaire weighing in on German politics”.

While the AfD’s ascendance has more to do with Germany’s domestic politics and social dynamics than it does with Musk, it did not stop him from taking some credit for their success. Musk reposted a claim from a Germany rightwing media commentator that the tech billionaire’s ownership of X had caused a “vibe shift” that led to the AfD’s victory.

In the days after the AfD’s election success in the state of Saxony-Anhalt, Musk both celebrated the result and tried to claim that the party was not far-right at all but ideologically moderate. Musk posted that the party, which Germany’s own domestic intelligence agency last year labeled a rightwing extremist group, should be considered “far center”.

Musk also sought to reject American news media’s descriptions of the AfD being far-right, despite the party’s well-documented and extreme views on issues such as immigration, Islam and LGBTQ+ rights. Musk posted multiple replies to the Wall Street Journal and CBS News following the state election, attacking the outlets for using “far right” in their coverage.

“You are lying by calling AfD ‘far-right’,” Musk responded to a CBS News post on X, adding in another post that “‘far right’ is a propaganda term”.

The AfD party platform includes bans on public displays of Islamic beliefs; opposes same-sex marriage and adoption, despite Weidel’s long-term domestic partnership with a woman, which includes children; emphasizes ethnic-German identity and calls for mass deportations. AfD leaders also have received criticism over the years for downplaying the Holocaust and making provocative references to Nazism, with one of the party’s top members convicted in 2024 of using a Nazi paramilitary wing slogan during a rally.

Weidel has meanwhile claimed there is “a holy war against the German population” while calling for “remigration”, a term for mass expulsions once popular in far-right and white nationalist circles that has now been embraced by nativist parties as well as Musk and Donald Trump.

Germany’s Chancellor Friedrich Merz responded to the AfD’s win this week by warning that the party’s true goals amounted to ethnic cleansing, a characterization which the far-right party denounced.

“If what is being advocated here, namely ‘remigration’, were to become reality, ⁠it would be nothing other than a synonym for ethnic cleansing based on origin and skin colour,” Merz said.

Musk once again defended the AfD, reposting a user criticising Merz’s allegation to his more than 241m followers.

Musk’s views, which include a fixation on race and vocal opposition to immigration, have come to closely resemble those of Weidel and the AfD.

“Anyone who opposes remigration is a traitor,” he posted in July.
